en: The Blessed Lord said: But this most secret knowledge I shall declare to you, who are free from malice.
That knowledge, accompanied by discernment, having known which you shall be liberated from evil. //1//
Śrīdhara:
It was established in the eighth chapter that the Supreme Lord is attained through pure devotion;
in the ninth, however, His most wonderful sovereignty is elaborated upon.

Having thus stated that the seventh and eighth [tattvas]— one's own supreme reality belonging to the Lord— are accessible only through devotion and not otherwise, the Blessed One now spoke these words, intending to elaborate upon His own inconceivable sovereignty and the extraordinary power of devotion.

"Vijñāna" (higher knowledge) is that by which something is known with distinction; it is worship accompanied by such knowledge, having the Lord as its object. But this [teaching] repeatedly instructs only My own majesty to one who is free from envy—that is, to one who is devoid of the perception of faults in Me, the supremely compassionate.
I shall speak to you;
the word "tu" (but/however) indicates a distinction. //1//

Madhusūdana: In the preceding chapter, it was described how for one whose vital breaths have departed at will through yoga— characterized by the restraint of all the doors of the senses and accompanied by concentration (*dhāraṇā*) on the crown of the head via the channel-less path, as well as on the heart, throat, the space between the eyebrows, and so forth—
the attainment of the Supreme Brahman at the end of the kalpa occurs through the arising of perfect knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) there in the world of Brahmā (*brahma-loka*).

The gradual liberation has been explained. Fearing that liberation might not be attained there by this very method and in no other way, [the Lord] stated that direct attainment of liberation results from the realization of the true nature of the Blessed One, beginning with: "For him who constantly and eternally remembers me with an undistracted mind, I am easily attained," and so forth.
And in that regard, it has been stated that exclusive devotion (*ananyā bhakti*) is the extraordinary cause: "That Supreme Person, O Pārtha, is attainable by means of undivided devotion" (8.22).

Now, the ninth chapter begins for the purpose of attaining liberation directly—without the distress of the previously mentioned practices such as yogic concentration (*dhāraṇā*), the departure of the vital breath (*prāṇotkramaṇa*), or traveling along the path of the rays of light (*arcir-ādi-mārga*) involving temporal delay—and for the sake of explaining the reality of the Blessed One in detail.
In the eighth chapter, by defining Brahman as the object of meditation, the destiny of one steadfast in that meditation was described;
in the ninth, however, by defining Brahman as the object of knowledge, the destiny of one steadfast in knowledge is stated—this is the summary.
Therein, three verses are intended to praise the knowledge that is about to be explained.

I shall declare to you this knowledge—which has been explained in many ways previously, which will be explained further on, and which is being stated now—whose authority is the sacred word (*śabda-pramāṇa*) and whose object is the reality of Brahman.
The word "but" (*tu*) indicates the distinction of this knowledge from the meditation (*dhyāna*) mentioned in the preceding chapter.
This alone is right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), the direct means for attaining liberation, and not meditation, because meditation does not remove ignorance.
It has been stated that this very knowledge, by means of purifying the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), brings about liberation gradually once it has been accomplished.

What kind of knowledge? It is the "most secret" (*guhyatama*), meaning most worthy of concealment because of its extreme esoteric nature; for it is accompanied by realized wisdom (*vijñāna*) and culminates in the direct experience of Brahman.
Although such a matter is an extreme secret, I shall speak it to you because of your excellence as a disciple and because you are free from envy (*anasūya*).
Envy (*asūyā*) is the perception of faults in virtues, resulting in their exposure and so forth;
it takes the form of always praising oneself by proclaiming one's own spiritual sovereignty in my presence. [I speak this] to one who is devoid of that.
By this, *ārjava* (straightforwardness) and *saṃyama* (self-restraint) are also explained as qualities of a disciple.

Furthermore, what kind of knowledge is it, knowing which—and attaining which—you shall be liberated immediately from the inauspicious bondage of worldly existence, which is the cause of all suffering? //1//
Viśvanātha:
In the ninth [chapter], it is clearly stated that the sovereignty required by the Lord’s servants for the purpose of worship, as well as the excellence of pure devotion, are described.
The superiority of devotion alone over action, knowledge,
yoga, and so forth has been stated in the seventh and eighth [chapters], where it is said that devotion is both predominant and exclusive (*kevalā*).
Even therein, the absolute superiority of exclusive devotion— which is exceedingly powerful and, like knowledge, does not depend on the purification of the internal organ and the like— is made clear.
The ninth chapter is commenced in order to describe the sovereignty required for that [state].

Of the Gītā scripture, which is the essence of all scriptures, the middle group of six chapters alone is the essence; of those as well, the ninth and tenth chapters are the very core. Therefore, with the three verses beginning "But this," he praises the subject matter that is about to be defined here.
That secret knowledge concerning the means to liberation which was taught in the second and third chapters and elsewhere,
and that even more secret knowledge regarding the means to attaining Me— which is known as the knowledge of the reality of the Lord and the reality of devotion (*bhakti*)— have been explained.
Now, however, I shall declare to you preeminently this most secret knowledge, characterized solely by pure devotion.
In this context, however, the word "knowledge" (jñāna) must necessarily be explained as devotion (bhakti),
and not as the well-known knowledge described in the first six chapters; for,

because the subsequent verse provides the qualifiers "imperishable" (avyaya) and "unchanging" (anaśvara), and thereby attains the state of transcending the qualities (guṇātītatva), it refers specifically to devotion that has transcended the qualities.
But knowledge is not [excluded],
because it is characterized by *sattva*.
Furthermore, in the subsequent verse, "Men who lack faith in this dharma," the word *dharma* refers specifically to devotion (*bhakti*).
By the words "to one who is free from envy" and "free from malice," the injunction is implied that another person should also teach this only to one who is free from malice.
The meaning is: accompanied by discernment (*vijñāna*) up to the limit of direct personal experience (*aparokṣānubhava*).
[It is taught] for the sake of liberation from the impure cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), which is an obstacle and hindrance to devotion.
Baladeva:
In the ninth [chapter], Hari spoke of His own wonderful supreme sovereignty which causes the kindling of devotion, as well as the great excellence of His own devotees.

Having declared in the seventh verse and those following that "I am the Lord of all, a mass of consciousness and bliss, a repository of countless jewels of auspicious qualities, and easily attained through pure devotion," he now— about to describe His own sovereignty which kindles devotion and the power of that devotion—
first praises it with three verses beginning with "This."
This knowledge consists of devotion characterized by chanting my names and so forth;
for it is said, "of this dharma [which exists] in another," and because chanting and the rest are functions of the power of consciousness (cic-chakti).
And according to the etymology, "that by which [something] is known" (jñāyate 'nena);
that indeed is the most secret.
The meaning is that the knowledge of My sovereignty taught from the second chapter onwards is even more secret.
The meaning is that in the ninth chapter and those following, this knowledge characterized solely by devotion—which is the most secret—is to be taught.
And I shall declare to you that [knowledge], accompanied by realized wisdom (vijñāna) and culminating in My direct experience.
To whom [is it to be taught]? He says: "to those who are free from envy."

The meaning is: "to one who is free from attributing faults to my qualities"—that is, to me, who out of compassion instructs you in my own difficult-to-comprehend secret, you praise yourself by proclaiming your own sovereignty;
thus it is shown that another person might also speak this to one who is free from envy.
Knowing which, you shall be liberated from this impure cycle of existence. //1//
This is the royal science, the royal secret, the supreme purifier; it is directly perceivable, consistent with dharma, very easy to practice, and imperishable. (9.2)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the royal science":
this knowledge is the royal science (*rājavidyā*), the king of all sciences;
it is the royal secret (*rājahṛdaya*), the king of all secrets.
The meaning is that among sciences and secrets, it is the most hidden and the best.
Due to its inclusion in the *rājadaṇḍādi* group, the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) is placed last;
thus it means either "the science of kings" or "the secret of kings."
This is the supreme purifier, the ultimate sanctifier; it is directly perceived by the wise— that is,
that whose comprehension and realization are immediate and clear.
The meaning is that its fruit is visible;
it is "righteous" (dharmya), meaning not departing from dharma,
because it yields the fruits of all the duties prescribed in the Vedas.
And "easy to perform" means that it is capable of being performed;
and it is "imperishable" because its fruit is inexhaustible. //2//

Madhusūdana: Furthermore, in order to induce him toward that [knowledge], He praises that knowledge with the words "O King. It is the *rāja-vidyā* because it is the king of all sciences (*vidyā*), owing to its power to destroy all forms of ignorance (*avidyā*);
for other sciences are only opposed to a single portion of ignorance.
Likewise, *rāja-guhya* is the king of all secrets;
because it is to be accomplished through the merit performed over many lifetimes, it is unknown by many.
The placement of the subordinate member at the end [of the compound] follows the rule for *rāja-danta* and similar formations.
This is indeed the supreme purification; for by means of expiations, only a single sin is averted.
And even when averted, it remains in its own cause in a subtle form, because of which the person accumulates that sin once again.
This, however, is the immediate destroyer of all sins—whether gross or subtle—accumulated over many thousands of births, as well as their cause, which is ignorance.
Therefore, this alone is the most excellent purifier.

Furthermore, unlike dharma, which is beyond the senses, there is no doubt for anyone regarding this [practice] either in its essential nature or its result, because it is directly perceived; thus he says: "It is understood through direct perception."

"Understanding" (*avagama*) means "that by which understanding is attained"; thus, *avagama* is the fruit. "Direct perception" (*pratyakṣa-avagama*) is the instrument of knowledge; "in this [instrument] there is direct perception" refers to its being directly perceived by the witness (*sākṣi*) in its own nature.
"Direct perception is its understanding" refers to its being directly perceived by the witness as a result.
For it is a universal witness-experience that one thinks: "I have known this, therefore my ignorance regarding this has now perished."

Thus, although it is established through worldly experience, that knowledge is *dharmya*—not departing from *dharma*—and is the fruit of the desireless *dharma* accumulated over many births. [Objection: In that case, it must be difficult to accomplish. [Reply: No; he says it is very easy to perform. It can be easily accomplished by means of the Vedāntic statements aided by the investigation shown by the Guru; it does not depend on the intervention of place, time, and so forth, because it is dependent solely upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object itself (*vastu*).

[Objection: "If knowledge were thus achievable without effort, it would yield only a small fruit, for we observe that only actions accomplished with great effort produce great fruits. [Reply: To this he says, "inexhaustible" (*avyayam*).
Even though this is achievable without effort, there is no exhaustion of its fruit; thus, "inexhaustible" means it possesses undecaying fruit.

But by means of action, even for the most great [beings], there is only the state of having perishable fruits; for the Śruti states: "O Gārgī, he who, not knowing this Imperishable, offers oblations, performs sacrifices, and practices austerities in this world for many thousands of years—all that belongs to him becomes finite" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.10).
Therefore, because it is the most excellent of all, the knowledge of the Self must indeed be trusted. //2//
Viśvanātha: Furthermore, this knowledge is *rājavidyā*. "Vidyā" refers to various forms of worship (*upāsanā*) and diverse types of devotion (*bhakti*); it is the king (*rājā*) among them.
The compound is placed with the final member first (*paranipāta*) according to the rule beginning with *rājadanta* (Pāṇini 2.2.31).
"King of secrets"—the mere devotion [to Him] is already extremely secret; that He is the "King" of even those manifold secrets is the most secret of all.
"This is purifying"—because it serves as the expiation for all sins and because it bestows purity even more than the knowledge of the meaning of the word *tvaṃ* (Thou).
It is the immediate destroyer of all sins—whether gross or subtle—accumulated over thousands of births, as well as their cause, which is ignorance.
Therefore, the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī says that this alone is the most excellent means of purification;
it is that whose realization and experience are direct and immediate.
Devotion is the experience of the Supreme Lord, and dispassion is...
Moreover, this triad occurs at one and the same time for one who is attaining [liberation],
just as for one eating there may be satisfaction, nourishment, and the removal of hunger with every morsel.
Thus, for the eleventh type of devotee, at every step there is the attainment of the experience of the Lord in accordance with their devotion;
this is "righteous" (*dharmyam*), meaning not departing from *dharma*, because even when no specific religious duty is performed, all duties are accomplished—
just as by watering the root of a tree [the whole plant thrives].
The branches that are the limbs of those aggregates are satisfied by the offering of life-force; just as the senses are satisfied by the sacrifice of breath,
so too is every form of worship performed for Acyuta.

Thus it is stated by Nārada. "Very easy to perform" means that, unlike in the case of ritual action (*karma*) or knowledge (*jñāna*), there is no excessive affliction of body, speech, or mind here; for devotion consisting of hearing, chanting, and so forth, is merely the activity of the sense organs such as the ears.
It is "imperishable" (*avyayam*), meaning it is not subject to destruction like ritual action or knowledge, because it is devoid of the material qualities (*nirguṇatvāt*). //2//
Baladeva: "The king of sciences" (*rāja-vidyā*):
among the sciences—those preceded by such terms as *Śāṇḍilya*, *Vaiśvānara*, and *Dahara*—this is the king, the supreme science.

"The king of secrets" (*rāja-guhya*): among the secrets—the esoteric truths concerning the true nature of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) and so forth—this knowledge in the form of devotion is the king.
Due to its inclusion in the *rājadaṇḍādi* group, the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) is placed at the end [of the compound].
To demonstrate this state, he qualifies it as "the supreme purifier" because it pacifies all sins extending even to the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*).
As it is said in the *Pādma*:
"The sin whose fruit has not yet begun, like a seed with its sprout ready to emerge,
is dissolved in due order for those whose souls delight in devotion to Viṣṇu.
Here, the sequence should be understood as being like the piercing of a hundred leaves one by one.
"Direct perception" (*pratyakṣāvagama*) refers to that which is perceived; that is, the object (*viṣaya*).
When that [object] exists within direct perception—such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth—while being practiced, I, the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*), manifest as its object.
Thus the author of the Sūtras says: "And there is manifestation in the practice of the action."

Righteous (dharmya) means not departing from dharma, being constantly nourished by duties such as service to the guru; "scripture" refers to such passages as "A person who has a teacher knows," and so forth; "easy to perform" means easily accomplished.
Because it consists merely of the operation of the ears and other senses, and because its requisites consist of nothing more than a vessel of *tulasī* and a handful of water;
and because it is imperishable (*avyaya*), persisting even in liberation (*mokṣa*).
Thus he will say: "By devotion one comes to know Me," and so forth.

But karma-yoga and the like are not such; therefore, this is a "royal science" (*rāja-vidyā*). Regarding this, they say: it is the science of kings, the secret of kings—meaning that this science belongs to those of noble mind like kings, or rather to compassionate ones who hold even heaven in contempt, and not to those who quickly worship the gods out of a desire for sons and other worldly gains.

For kings, even when possessing great wealth such as jewels, do not conceal their own counsel; rather, they strive with extreme effort to conceal it. Likewise, my devotees—though not concealing other sciences—should conceal this one with the utmost effort, lest those of dejected mind who perform ritual acts should discover it.
The rest is the same. //2//
O scorcher of foes, those persons who lack faith in this dharma do not reach Me, but return to the path of the mortal cycle of rebirth. (9.3)
Śrīdhara: [Objection: "If this is so easy to perform, who indeed would remain worldly transmigrators?
To this he says: "Those lacking faith," referring to this [path] characterized by knowledge accompanied by devotion.
The word "dharmasya" is used in the accusative sense.

Those who lack faith in this dharma— that is, those who do not accept it with conviction— even though they exert effort through other means for the sake of attaining Me, fail to reach Me and return to the path of worldly existence characterized by death.
The meaning is that they wander about on the path of saṃsāra, which is pervaded by death. //3//

Madhusūdana: [Objection: If this [path] is so easy to perform and so supremely excellent, why do all people not engage in it? And if they did, no one would remain in saṃsāra. To this, he says: "those who lack faith" (aśraddadhānāḥ). This means that even though the nature, the means, and the fruit of this dharma called self-knowledge have been expounded in the scriptures, those who lack faith in them...
With their inner faculties corrupted by the perception of fallacious arguments that contradict the Vedas, they do not regard [the scriptures] as authoritative.

Being evildoers who have ascended to the state of the *asuras*, even though they strive somehow by means of methods devised by their own intellect, they turn back—meaning they remain fixed in their failure—because they lack the means prescribed by the scripture; thus, failing to reach Me, they do not even obtain the means for attaining Me.

The meaning is: "Where, on the path of saṃsāra joined with death, they constantly wander through the continuous succession of birth and death in the very wombs of hell-beings, animals, and so forth. //3//
Viśvanātha: [Objection: But if this [knowledge] were thus to produce such extreme happiness, who indeed would remain a transmigrating being?
To this he says: "those who lack faith.
Here, the genitive case in *asya* (of this) is used in the sense of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*), according to the archaic usage (*ārṣī*).

Those who, lacking faith in this teaching established by the words of the scriptures, consider the supreme excellence of devotion to be merely a figurative eulogy and do not accept it with conviction—they, even though they have exerted effort toward attaining Me through other means, fail to reach Me and remain most excessively on the path of worldly existence pervaded by death. //3//
Baladeva: If it is argued that "in this way, since the Dharma is so easy to practice, no one at all would wander in saṃsāra," he says in response, "those who lack faith" (*aśraddadhānāḥ*).
The word *dharmasya* is used in the accusative sense (denoting the object).

Those who lack faith—even in this Dharma characterized by devotion to Me, whose power is well-known from the Vedas and other sources—do not grasp it with firm conviction; rather, they think, "This is merely a matter of praise."

Even though they practice other means for the sake of attaining Me, because they disregard devotion, they fail to reach Me and remain deeply entrenched on the path of worldly existence joined with death. //3//
By Me, whose form is unmanifest, all this world is pervaded; all beings abide in Me, yet I do not dwell in them. (9.4)

Śrīdhara: Thus, having directed the listener's attention by praising the knowledge that was introduced as the subject to be explained, he speaks of that very knowledge in two verses beginning with "by me.
"Whose form"—that is, whose nature—is unmanifest and beyond the senses;
by me, being such a cause, this entire world is pervaded.
"Having created that, He entered into that very thing," according to such scriptural passages.
Therefore, all beings—both moving and non-moving—abide in Me, who am their cause; thus they are said to "reside in Me.
Nevertheless, just as clay does not reside within its effects such as jars, I do not abide within those beings.
Because it is unattached, like space. //4//

Madhusūdana: Thus, having directed Arjuna toward the praise of that very knowledge which was promised as the subject to be spoken of—both by way of positive injunction and by way of the negation of others—he speaks of that same knowledge in two verses beginning with "By Me":
"This entire world," consisting of all beings and their material components, along with their causes—the totality of the perceptible—is imagined through My ignorance (māyā).

"How can the entire world be pervaded by you, Vāsudeva, who are limited [in form], given the contradiction with direct perception? [The world] is pervaded— that is, permeated— by that which is the ultimate reality, whose nature is existence and whose nature is manifestation, through the sustaining power of *māyā*, just as a rope-segment [pervades] the snake, the stream of water, and so forth, which are imagined by ignorance regarding it."

"No," he says; "by me—whose form is unmanifest, beyond the range of all the senses, and consisting of self-luminous non-dual consciousness and eternal bliss—all this is pervaded, and not by this body. This is the meaning.
Therefore, all beings, both stationary and moving, exist as if they were present, as if they were vibrating, abiding in my own form; they abide in me.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), however, I am not at all situated within those imagined elements (*bhūta*), because a connection between the imagined and the unimagined is impossible.
For this very reason it has been said: "That upon which something is superimposed is not connected by even an atom’s worth of quality or defect produced by that [superimposition]. //4//
Viśvanātha: With seven verses, [the Lord] states that this knowledge of My sovereignty alone is to be sought by My devotees regarding devotional service characterized by servitude (*dāsya-bhakti*).
By Me—whose form (*mūrti*) or essential nature (*svarūpa*) is unmanifest (*avyakta*) and beyond the senses (*atīndriya*)—as the causal ground, this entire universe is pervaded (*tataṃ*).
Therefore, all beings, both moving and unmoving, abide in Me; that is, they reside within Me, who am the causal ground and whose essential nature is perfect consciousness (*pūrṇa-caitanya*).
Even so, I do not abide in those elements such as the jar and the like—which are my own effects—just as one does not abide in deer and other animals, because of my state of non-attachment. //4//
Baladeva: Now, with the words "by Me," He describes His own wonderful sovereignty which kindles devotion to Himself.
By Me—whose form (mūrti) is unmanifest (avyakta), meaning whose nature is beyond the grasp of the senses—this entire world is pervaded (tataṃ) for the purpose of supporting and controlling it.

Therefore, all beings, both moving and non-moving, abide in Me, who am all-pervading, the supporter, and the controller; the meaning is that their existence is not independent, but rather dependent upon Him.
In this context, it has been stated that "I, as the inner controller of the entire world, having entered within by means of My own portion, govern and sustain [it].
And so says the Śruti: "He who dwells in the earth," and so forth. Here too, the Lord will say: "Pervading all this," and so forth. //4//
And yet, beings do not abide in Me; behold My divine yoga!
My Self, the source of all beings, sustains beings but does not dwell within them. (9.5)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore,
"nor do beings abide in me," because of my very state of non-attachment.
Anticipating the objection that "in that case, the previously mentioned [attributes of] being all-pervasive and having a locus are contradictory," he says, "Behold.
Behold my sovereignty, my uncommon yoga—that is, my skill in bringing about the impossible.
The meaning is: because the majesty of my yogic power (yoga-māyā) is inconceivable, nothing whatsoever is contradictory.
"Behold another marvel," he says with the word *bhūta*.
He who bears—that is, supports—the elements (*bhūta*) is *bhūta-bhṛt*;
he who nourishes—that is, protects—the elements is *bhūta-bhāvana*.
"Even though I am thus situated as the Supreme Self, I do not abide within the elements.

This is the meaning: just as the individual soul (jīva), while bearing and sustaining the body, remains conjoined with it through egoism (ahaṅkāra), so too, although I support and sustain the elements, I do not abide within them because I am free from egoism. //5//
Madhusūdana says: "Therefore, not so.

Just as the movements of water and other such phenomena are superimposed upon the sun situated in the sky, so too the elements superimposed upon Me do not exist in Me from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

You, Arjuna, having abandoned the ordinary human intellect, behold—contemplate—My yoga, My power, My divine sovereignty, and My skill in accomplishing the impossible, as you would observe that of a master illusionist.
The meaning is as follows:
"I am not to be supported by anyone, nor am I the support of anyone; nevertheless, that 'I am in all beings and all beings are in me'—this is a great illusion.
For [the Self] is the sustainer of beings (*bhūta-bhṛt*), because it bears, maintains, and nourishes all beings as their material cause (*upādāna*).
He is called the "evolver of beings" (*bhūta-bhāvana*) because he brings forth all beings as their agent.

Thus, although my Self is the undifferentiated material cause, it constitutes my ultimate nature (*paramārtha-svarūpa*). Being a mass of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*sac-cid-ānanda-ghana*), and because its nature is unattached and non-dual, it abides in beings; yet in the ultimate sense, it has no connection with beings, like one who observes a dream.
The meaning is that [the self] is not, in the ultimate sense, related to [the body] as one's own;
rather, the genitive case in "my self" (*mama ātmā*) is used through conceptual construction, like the expression "Rāhu’s head. //5//
Viśvanātha: Therefore, the meaning is that although all beings reside within Me, they do not abide in Me, precisely because of My lack of attachment (*asaṅgatva*).

[An objection: "In that case, Your previously stated omnipresence and being the substratum of the universe would be contradictory. To this He says: "Behold My divine yoga"—that is, My extraordinary power of yoga consisting of the skill of accomplishing the impossible—and He says further, "Behold another wonder": He sustains and supports all beings; thus He is the "supporter of beings" (*bhūta-bhṛt*).
He is called *bhūta-bhāvana* because he nourishes and protects all beings (*bhūtāni*).

Even though my Self (*ātman*) is of such a nature, it does not abide in the elements (*bhūta-stha*); thus, the use of the genitive in "my [Self]" (*mama ātmā*) is due to the absence of any distinction between the body and the embodied one in the Blessed One, just as the genitive is used in the expression "the head of Rāhu" despite there being no actual difference.

The meaning is this: just as a living being, while assuming and maintaining a body, remains situated within that very body due to attachment to it, so too I, while assuming and maintaining all beings, am not situated within them despite having all illusory beings as my body, because of my state of non-attachment. //5//
Baladeva: If it be argued that there would be great distress for you as you carry such an exceedingly heavy burden, he says "not so" (*na ca*) in response.
Just as water and other substances are not inherently present within a jar, the elemental beings (*bhūta*) that constitute the burden are not actually joined together within me.
If that were so, it would contradict the statement "all beings abide in me"; therefore, they do not exist [as a burden] in me.
If it is objected that the statement "all beings abide in Me" would then be contradictory, He says in response: "Behold.

Behold—that is, know—My divine, unique yoga. According to its etymology (*nirukti*), yoga is that by which one is joined to difficult-to-accomplish tasks; thus, it refers to the attribute whose nature is inconceivable power and is characterized by the realization of true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpatā*).
This is the meaning.
He clarifies this very point by saying "the sustainer of beings" (*bhūta-bhṛt*): I am the sustainer and protector of beings, yet I do not exist as one who is attached to or joined with beings.

For it is through Me—the Self, which is the mind itself—that I perform the sustaining and protecting of beings by means of the yoga of sovereignty characterized by the power of true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpatā*), and not by means of the activity of My own physical form; such is the meaning.

And the Śruti says thus: "O Gārgī, by the command of this Imperishable (akṣara), the sun and moon stand held apart; O Gārgī, by the command of this Imperishable, heaven and earth stand held apart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.9), and so forth.
Although the mind is not different from its own nature (svarūpa),...
Nevertheless, it should be understood that this was stated by taking into account a real effect of differentiation, just as in the case of [the statement] "existence exists" and so forth. //5//
Just as the great wind, all-pervading, eternally abides in space, even so understand that all beings abide in Me. (9.6)
Śrīdhara: He states the relationship of support and supported between two things that are not even joined by means of an illustration with the words "yayā" (by which).
Since it is impossible for air to exist without space, air—which, though all-pervading and vast, is eternally situated in space—does not become joined with space.
This is because, being partless, it is incapable of conjunction.
Likewise, know that all beings abide in me. //6//
Madhusūdana: With the word "yathā" (just as), he explains the relationship of support and supported between two things that are not physically joined by means of an illustration.

Just as the wind—which is always characterized by motion and therefore moves everywhere, being "sarvatraga"—is eternally situated in space, which is by nature unattached, so too [the Self is situated in the body]. At all times—during the periods of origination, maintenance, and dissolution—the wind is always of a mobile nature;
for this very reason, it goes everywhere, and thus it is called "sarvatraga."
It is great in its extent;

even such as this, it is never at any time conjoined with space. In the same way, understand and reflect upon this: within me, whose nature is non-attachment, all beings—beginning with space—are great and all-pervasive, yet they exist without any actual union with me, nor do they exist [as independent entities]. Thus, having reflected, you should ascertain this.

Viśvanātha: [The Lord] says "just as" (yathā) to provide an illustration for the point that although all beings reside in Me, who am unattached, they do not truly reside in Me, and although I reside in them, I do not truly reside in them. Just as the wind—which by its very nature is always in motion—resides eternally in space, whose nature is likewise unattached.

Therefore, because it goes everywhere, it is "all-pervading" (*sarvatraga*); it is "great" (*mahat*) in terms of its dimension, just as space is. Because of its non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*), although situated therein, it is not situated.

Just as space, though situated in the wind, is not situated precisely because of its non-attachment, so too, understand—having reflected and reached a firm conclusion—that all great and all-pervading elements, beginning with space, are situated in me, whose nature is non-attachment, yet they are not situated.
[Objection: In that case, how was it established that the divine power of yoga mentioned by the Blessed One in the words "Behold, then, my divine yoga" is beyond the reach of logic?
[Response: Because of the attainment of an illustrative example.
It is said: because space is insentient (*jaḍa*), it is unattached (*asaṅga*).

However, the unattached nature of the conscious being—given that the status of presiding over the foundation of the world cannot belong to anyone other than the Supreme Lord—is already established as inconceivable. Furthermore, the illustration of space should be understood as being intended solely for the purpose of entering into the common understanding of the world. //6//
Baladeva says: "The existence and activity of all beings, both moving and non-moving, are dependent upon My will; regarding this, He provides an illustration with the word 'just as' (yathā).

Just as the great wind, itself without support, remains in the vast, supportless sky and moves everywhere—understand that its supportless existence and its activity proceed solely from My will, according to the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa and other Vedic texts such as, 'From fear of Him the wind blows. (Bhagavad-gītā 9.10)
Likewise, understand that all beings, whether stationary or moving, abide in Me; they exist within Me, being satisfied by Me, supported by My mere volition alone, and eternally measured by Me.
Otherwise, space and the other elements would fall into disorder. //6//
O son of Kuntī, at the end of a kalpa all beings go to my own nature; again, at the beginning of a kalpa, I send them forth. (9.7)

Śrīdhara: Thus, it has been stated that even though He is unattached, He is the cause of the persistence [of the world] through His yoga-māyā. And with the words "sarva... (all), he states that by that very same [māyā], He is the cause of the effort toward creation:
at the end of the kalpa, during the time of dissolution, all beings go back to primordial nature (prakṛti).
They dissolve into Māyā, which consists of the three guṇas;
then, at the beginning of a kalpa, during the time of creation, I emit them—I create them specifically. //7//

Madhusūdana: Having thus stated that the unattached Self is not joined with the imagined phenomenal world (prapañca) at the time of its origination and its duration, He speaks of that same non-attachment even at the time of dissolution in the verse beginning with "sarvāṇi. At the end of the kalpa, during the time of dissolution, all beings go to My own Nature (prakṛti)—which is imagined as My power (māyā), consists of the three guṇas, and serves as their own cause; the meaning is that they dissolve right there in a subtle form.
"O Kaunteya"—the meaning of this has already been explained.

Furthermore, at the beginning of the kalpa, at the time of creation, I—the omniscient, omnipotent Lord—emit them; that is, I, the All-Knowing One, manifest those [beings] which had attained a state of non-distinction within primordial nature (prakṛti). //7//
Viśvanātha: [Objection: But now these visible beings are perceived as residing within you;
in response to the expectation of where they will go at the time of the great dissolution (mahā-pralaya), he says "all" and so forth.
The meaning is that they merge into my own—that is, mine—my power of illusion (māyā-śakti), which consists of the three qualities (triguṇa).
Furthermore, at the end of the dissolution at the conclusion of the kalpa, at the time of creation, I create them specifically. //7//
Baladeva: It has been stated that the maintenance of beings occurs solely through His own volition.
Now, with the words "sarva... and so forth, He describes their creation and dissolution from that very same source.
O Kaunteya!
At the end of the kalpa, at the time of the dissolution of the four-faced Brahmā, all beings go to my own nature solely through my volition;

they dissolve into me, who possess the power of primordial nature (prakṛti). Then, at the beginning of the kalpa, by my mere volition—"May I become manifold"—I create them again in their various forms. //7//
Taking hold of My own nature, I send forth again and again this entire multitude of beings, which is powerless under the sway of nature. (9.8)

Śrīdhara: Now, in response to the inquiry, "Since you are unattached and changeless, how do you create?", he says: "Prakṛtim" (the material nature). Having taken hold of—that is, presiding over—my own, which is under my control, *prakṛti*; I repeatedly create in various ways this entire fourfold collection of beings, which was merged during the dissolution and is subject to karma and other factors.
Or rather, [the Lord thinks], "I create with distinction.
How so? By the power of primordial nature (prakṛti), and by the power of the respective inherent natures caused by past karma. //8//

Madhusūdana: For what purpose does this creation abide in the Supreme Lord? It is certainly not for His own enjoyment, because He, being pure consciousness that is the witness of all, lacks the status of an enjoyer; for if that were the case, He would be a transmigrating soul (*saṃsārī*), which would contradict His nature as the Lord (*īśvara*). Nor is there another enjoyer for whose sake this creation exists.
Because there is no other volition;
because the Lord alone exists everywhere in the form of the individual soul (jīva);
and because that which is insentient cannot be an enjoyer.

Therefore, creation is not for the sake of liberation either, because there is no bondage [to be released] and because [creation] is contrary to liberation; thus, the initial logical inconsistency—which establishes that creation consists of *māyā*—is not unfavorable to us and need not be refuted. With this intention, the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) due to its being composed of *māyā* [is established].
He begins to speak with three verses, starting with "prakṛtim":

having taken hold of his own *prakṛti*— which is called *māyā*, is indefinable (*anirvacanīyā*), and is imagined within himself— and having strengthened it by means of his own existence and manifestation,

[he acts] by the power of that *prakṛti*, *māyā*, through the influence of its potencies consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and the veil (*āvaraṇa*) and distraction (*vikṣepa*) which are the causes of clinging (*abhiniveśa*).

I repeatedly emit—like a magician—and create in manifold ways through mere imagination this entire host of beings brought together by all the means of valid cognition, this collection of elements beginning with space, just as a dreamer creates the expansion of a dream. //8//
Viśvanātha: Now, in response to the inquiry, "Since you are unattached and changeless, how do you create?", he says: "Prakṛtim" (Prakṛti).
Having "avaṣṭabhya" (seized) or presided over "svām" (his own), that is, his own *prakṛti*; "prakṛter vaśāt" means by the power of his own nature, which is to say, due to the cause of past karma.
"Avaśam" means dependent on karma and other such factors. //8//
Baladeva says: "By 'Prakṛti'—

having taken hold of, that is, presiding over, my own Prakṛti consisting of the three guṇas, and having transformed the intellect (mahat) and the other principles by mere volition, I emit this fourfold collection of beings again and again at the appropriate times."

To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says: By the power—that is, the influence—of *prakṛti*, which consists of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of past actions, [the world] is "unwilling," meaning dependent on others.

Furthermore, for me, whose nature is unattached and whose power is inconceivable, who performs this or that by mere volition (*saṅkalpa*), there is not even a trace of contact with those [actions], nor is there the slightest bit of weariness. //8//
And those actions do not bind Me, O Dhanañjaya, for I remain as if indifferent, unattached to those actions. (9)

Śrīdhara: [Objection] "But surely, for you who perform such various kinds of actions, how is it that bondage does not occur as it does for an individual soul (jīva)? To this he says: "And they do not bind me. Those actions, such as the creation of the universe and so forth, do not bind me.

For attachment to action is indeed the cause of bondage, and that does not exist in me because my desires have been fulfilled. Therefore, since indifference is impossible for me, it was said that I stand "as if indifferent. //9//

Madhusūdana: Therefore, "nor do they bind Me. Nor indeed do those [functions] called creation, maintenance, and dissolution—performed by Me like a magician or like one seeing a dream—bind Me through favor or punishment, nor do they make Me a partaker of good or evil deeds, because they are illusory in nature.
"He [Dhanañjaya] conquered all the kings for the sake of King Yudhiṣṭhira’s Rājasūya sacrifice and brought back their wealth"—thus his great power is indicated for the purpose of encouragement.
To the question of why those actions do not bind him, he says: "He sits like one who is indifferent.

Just as some indifferent person, sitting between two disputants, remains untouched by victory or defeat and unaffected by the joy or sorrow produced thereby, remaining changeless—so too does he sit in a state of changelessness.
Since there is no dispute between these two here, the suffix *-vati* is used on the basis of their mere commonality of being indifferent (*upekṣakatva*).

Therefore, because they are changeless, it is entirely logical that actions do not bind Me—who am unattached to those acts of creation and so forth, and who am devoid of the attachment characterized by the conceit "I am doing"—even though I appear to act.
For it has been stated that for any other person as well, in the absence of agency and the absence of attachment to the fruit, actions are not causes of bondage.
But when both of these exist, the intention is that the fool is bound by karmas, just like the author of the Kośa. //9//
Viśvanātha: [Objection: But if this is so, how is it that you, who perform various actions, do not incur bondage like an individual soul (jīva)? To this he says, "And not...
[referring to] those [actions], such as creation and so forth.
For attachment to action is the cause of bondage, and that does not exist in me because my desires have been fulfilled.
"Like one who is indifferent" means:
just as another person who is indifferent is not affected by the suffering, grief, and so forth of those who are quarreling, even so am I; this is the meaning. //9//

Baladeva: [Objection: "But surely, the acts characterized by creation, maintenance, and destruction—being unequal—might bind you through partiality and the like. To this he says, "Not so" (*na ca*). Those actions, such as the unequal creation and so forth, do not occasion partiality and the like in Me. The reason for this is contained in the qualifying epithet "as if indifferent" (*udāsīnavat*).

The causes for living beings existing in the states of gods, humans, animals, and so forth, as well as for the varying degrees of their respective prosperity, are solely their previously accumulated karmas.
However, because I remain impartial toward those diverse karmas and am unattached, there is not even a trace of defects such as partiality in Me.
Thus the author of the Sūtras has stated: "Partiality and cruelty [are not attributed to the Lord], etc. (VS 2.1.35).
If one were truly indifferent, agency would not be established; therefore it is said, "as if indifferent. //9//
Under my supervision, Nature produces the world of the moving and the unmoving;
by this cause, O son of Kuntī, the universe revolves. 9.10

Śrīdhara explains that very point with the words "by me": "By me, acting as the supervisor and the instrumental cause, primordial nature (prakṛti) brings forth—the world consisting of the moving and the non-moving—and gives birth to it.
By this reason of my supervision, this universe revolves, being born again and again."
The sense is that because he is the presiding controller by mere proximity, his status as the agent and his state of neutrality are not contradictory. //10//

Madhusūdana: To dispel the doubt that the statements "I emit this multitude of beings" and "remaining as if indifferent" are mutually contradictory, he once again reveals the nature of [the world] as consisting of *māyā* with the word "by me.
By me—whose essential nature is pure consciousness alone, who am changeless, the presiding witness, the controller, and the illuminator—is *prakṛti* manifested.
Māyā, which consists of the three guṇas and is indefinable as being either existent or non-existent, gives birth to— the world with its moving and unmoving beings—
just as Māyā presided over by a magician produces imagined elephants, horses, and so forth.
However, I do not perform any other activity apart from the manifestation of Māyā, which is my own effect.

O Kaunteya, by this cause, this motive—namely, this state of being the Supreme Overseer (adhyakṣatva)—the world, including all that is moving and unmoving, revolves in its various ways, from birth to destruction, like the sun and other celestial bodies. Since there is an absence of agency [on His part], it was said that He "sits as if indifferent"; thus, there is no contradiction.
As it has been said:
"Depending upon that ignorance which is the material cause of this net of duality, Brahman is called the cause.
In this regard, thousands of statements from Śruti and Smṛti may be cited. (10)
Viśvanātha: [Objection: "Indeed, I do not believe in this indifference of yours who are the agent of creation and so forth. To this he says: "By me.
With me as the presiding cause, *prakṛti* produces the world with its moving and non-moving beings.
It is *prakṛti* alone that generates the world.
My role here is merely that of a presiding witness.
Just as in the case of a certain king, such as Ambarīṣa, where the affairs of state are carried out by the subjects alone, the king remains indifferent;
it is his mere presence that matters, for without his mere presence upon the royal throne, nothing can be accomplished by the subjects.
In the same way, the meaning is that even primordial nature (*prakṛti*), being insentient, is unable to do anything at all without my characteristic of presiding over it as the supervisor.
By this cause of my presiding, this world revolves, being born again and again. //10//
Baladeva explains this with the words "by me":

"By me—the Lord of all, whose will is ever true, and who is the presiding overseer of primordial nature (prakṛti)—nature, when beheld by me in accordance with the prior karma of each individual soul, gives birth to and produces the world of moving and non-moving beings;
being composed of the unequal qualities (guṇas), that world revolves again and again, arising anew through this cause of my vision, which conforms to the prior karma of the souls."
O Kaunteya,
and the Śruti says this as well:
"The unborn, eternal, eightfold Prakṛti, which is ignorance, the producer of transformations."
It is meditated upon by Him, and being presided over by Him, it is expanded;
furthermore, impelled by Him, it brings forth the world, and governed by Him alone, it produces the goals of human existence.
Thus, because He exercises lordship through mere proximity (*sannidhi-mātra*), His status as the agent (*kartṛtva*) and His state of indifference (*udāsīnatva*) are not contradictory.
Just as it is remembered that fragrance causes agitation [of the mind] through mere proximity, so too, this very fact—that Nature (*prakṛti*) requires my mere lordship—is established.
Without me, she would not be capable of accomplishing anything; for indeed, in the absence of a king’s presiding over the throne, his ministers have no power to act. //10//
Fools disregard me when I have assumed a human form,
being ignorant of my supreme nature as the Great Lord of all beings. (9.11)
Śrīdhara: But why is it that some do not respect You, the Supreme Lord who are such as this? To this he replies with two verses beginning with "They disregard.
Being ignorant of my supreme nature—the reality—which is the form of the Great Lord of all beings, these deluded fools disregard me; they treat me with contempt.
The reason for this disregard is that [the Lord], although his body consists of pure sattva, has assumed a human form by the power of the desire of his devotees. //11//

Madhusūdana: Thus, although my nature is eternally pure, enlightened, and liberated, and although I am the Self of all beings—consisting of solid bliss and infinite—they disregard me. These deluded people, lacking discrimination, do not respect me, thinking, "This is merely a human being," or they even revile me. He points out the error that is the cause of their disregard: that I have assumed a human body and am perceived as a mere man.
[He is] one who has assumed a form by His own will for the sake of favoring His devotees, meaning He conducts Himself through a body that appears as human;
and thus, those whose inner faculties are shrouded by the delusion that "this is a mere man" [do not perceive] My supreme state, which is most excellent.
That they do not respect or even revile the ultimate reality—the Great Lord who dwells within all beings—is entirely consistent with their state of delusion. //11//

Viśvanātha: Indeed, it is true that you are that very one who is renowned as the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa), pervading infinite millions of universes, whose form is existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda), who reclines upon the causal ocean, and who creates the world by means of his own nature.
However, because some speak of Your degradation on the mere grounds that "this human body belongs to the son of Vasudeva," He says: "Those who disregard Me.
They are indeed ignorant of the supreme nature of this human body of Mine—its true essence—which is superior even to the Great Person reclining upon the causal ocean and other such forms.
Of what nature is it? It is both the *bhūtam*, the real, which is Brahman, and the *maheśvaram*, the Great Lord.

In this context, that state of Maheśvara should be understood as excluding other [lower] levels of reality; for Amara states: "The term *bhūta* is used when the earth and so forth are joined with the element.

Thus, according to the Śruti: "I, together with the hosts of Maruts, constantly satisfy that one Govinda, whose form is existence-consciousness-bliss (*sac-cid-ānanda*), who sits beneath the celestial trees of Vṛndāvana, with the highest hymn of praise" (GTU 1.33).

And because of the traditional teaching that "the Supreme Brahman has a human form," the fact that this human body of Mine consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss is indeed declared by My devotees who possess direct realization; likewise, its pervasion of the entire universe was witnessed even by Śrī Yaśodā when she saw Me as a mere infant.

Or rather, he qualifies the human body itself as being the supreme state (*paraṃ bhāvam*), which means a pure existence (*viśuddhaṃ sattvam*) whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda-svarūpa*).
According to Amara, "state" (*bhāvaḥ*) means existence (*sattā*) or essential nature (*svabhāva*).
He further qualifies that supreme state as my Great Lord of beings (*mama bhūta-maheśvaram*); that is, the great Lord even of those beings to be created by me, such as Brahmā and the others.
Therefore, just as with the individual soul (jīva), my body is not distinct from me, the Supreme Lord;

I am indeed the body, and the body is indeed I—verily Brahman itself, possessing a form that embodies the Brahman of scripture. This is the sense in which you, like Śuka who knew Me, should have faith. Thus is the intention.
Baladeva: But why do some fail to respect you, who possess such majesty? To this he replies with the words "They disregard me.
Those fools disregard me—who am the Great Lord of all beings, the sole Sovereign of the entire universe, whose resolve is ever-true, who am omniscient, and supremely compassionate.
Showing the manner in this context, he qualifies [the subject] with the word "mānuṣīm" (human-like), meaning:

some person of fierce merit, regarding me—who have eternally attained [this state] through the relation of identity by resorting to a body that is a glorious form (*śrī-mūrti*) characterized by a human configuration and abounding in human gestures—as being equal to any other royal prince, treats me with contempt, thinking, "This is merely a human being. This is the meaning.
Indeed, a human body is composed of the five elements, whereas the body of the Blessed One is not like that, being of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*);
for it is heard in scripture that "Govinda alone is the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Were it otherwise, those who would despise Him would be joined with the blindness of folly, and He could not possibly be the object of worship for Brahmā and the other gods.
From what source, then, does their understanding arise such that they are called "deluded"?
To this he says: "The Supreme" (param). This means:

not knowing the supreme, unique state or nature—that is, because of their lack of acquaintance with His nature as consisting of knowledge and bliss, as being the Lord of all, and as the giver of liberation, despite His having a human form.

This being the case, one should understand that the effect of differentiation—which is manifested through the specific expression "resorting to a subtle body" (tanum āśritam)—is taken up [as the basis for this distinction].
For the true nature of the son of Vasudeva, the lord of Dvārakā, was manifest in the lying-in chamber itself as four-armed;
however, his form while going from there to Vraja was human and two-armed. Therefore, it is said: "He became an ordinary infant," and so forth.

Because of his statement, "There exists that [Supreme Being] who has taken recourse to a human body," and because of Pārtha’s words, "In that very form as four-armed [Viṣṇu]," it is therefore stated that the very fact of that body being arranged in a human manner constitutes its humanity, wherein the Supreme Brahman known as Kṛṣṇa has descended in human form.
In the *Śrī-vaiṣṇava* it is said: "The supreme Brahman is hidden within the human form," and in the *Śrī-bhāgavata*:
"And because of the abundance of human activities, that is its true nature."
Just as a human being who acts like a god or like a lion is designated as a "god among men" (nṛ-deva) or a "lion among men" (nṛ-siṃha), so too,
by virtue of the two aforementioned reasons, he— whether two-armed or four-armed— is designated according to his human nature.
Indeed, divinity does not depend on the abundance of arms.
Because there is a deviation [from the rule] in the case of Kārtavīrya and others;
for "supremacy" consists in being all-pervading consciousness or being the cause of the world's birth and so forth,
and that indeed exists in Him who has two arms, as is heard in scripture, yet His state of having two arms is not something that began in time (sādi).
"Having six lotus-like eyes, cloud-like in appearance, with lightning for a garment,
two-armed, rich in the gesture of silence (mauna-mudrā), and wearing a garland of forest flowers— [such is] the Lord.

Because of this scriptural testimony regarding His being established from beginningless time, the phrase "an ordinary child" (*prākṛtaḥ śiśuḥ*) means that He is a child manifested by His very nature (*prakṛtyā*), that is, by His essential form (*svarūpeṇa*).

Therefore, just as various forms appear in a lapis lazuli gem, the states of being two-armed and so forth are established simultaneously within Him and may be worshipped according to one's preference; thus, the conceptualizations of "peaceful" versus "arisen" or "perpetually arisen" are cast far aside.
(BhG 9.12) "Those whose hopes are vain, whose actions are vain, whose knowledge is vain, and who are senseless..."
They have resorted to a delusive nature that is both demonic and asuric. //12//
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "those whose hopes are vain": those whose hopes—such as the thought that another deity besides Me will quickly grant results—are vain, meaning fruitless;
for this very reason, because they are turned away from Me, their ritual actions are also vain, meaning fruitless.
Those whose knowledge of the scriptures is entirely in vain, being based on various fallacious arguments, are for that very reason "devoid of sense," meaning their minds are distracted.

The cause for this everywhere is that they have resorted to a *prakṛti*—an inherent nature—that is demonic (*rākṣasī*), characterized by darkness (*tāmasī*) and abounding in violence and the like; and asuric (*āsuri*), characterized by passion (*rājasī*) and full of lust, pride, and so forth—a deluding nature that causes the ruin of the intellect.
"Being dependent [on Me], they disregard Me"—this is the connection with what precedes. //12//

Madhusūdana: And they—whose intellects are obstructed by the great evil produced by their contempt for and reviling of the Blessed Lord, and who are thus destined for an uninterrupted residence in hell—are "those whose hope is vain" (moghāśāḥ).
This means those whose hope—that is, their prayer for results—consists in the vain and fruitless notion that "karmas alone will grant us their fruit, even without a Lord.
For this very reason, because they are turned away from the Lord, their karmas such as the *agnihotra* and others are "vain," being merely a form of labor.

Likewise, they are those whose knowledge is born of fallacious reasoning and treatises that do not establish the Lord; for what reason is this so? Because they are "devoid of discernment," meaning their discriminative wisdom is obstructed by the evil produced from their contempt for the Blessed One. Furthermore, by virtue of that contempt for the Blessed One, they possess a demonic, tamasic nature, characterized primarily by hatred and unordained violence.

They indeed resort to an asuric and rajasic nature—a disposition characterized by passion for the enjoyment of objects not sanctioned by the scriptures, which is delusive and causes the loss of scriptural knowledge. And therefore: "This threefold gate of hell, which is the destruction of the self,"
The meaning is that, because desire, anger, and greed are said to be the very gates to hell, they constantly experience the torments of hell itself. //12//

Viśvanātha: Now, as for those who, thinking "this Lord has assumed a human body composed of illusion," despise You—for them, what is their fate? To this he says: "Their hopes are in vain" (moghāśāḥ). Even if they were devotees, their hopes would nonetheless be in vain.
They do not attain my desired states, such as *sālokya* (residing in the same world).
If they are performers of ritual action (*karmiṇaḥ*), then they are of futile action, for they do not obtain the fruit of action, such as heaven and the like.
If they are possessors of knowledge (*jñāninaḥ*), then they are of futile knowledge, for they do not find liberation, which is the fruit of knowledge.
If so, what do they obtain? To this he says: "the demonic" (rākṣasīm).
The meaning is that they resort to, that is, they attain, the demonic nature—the inherent character of Rākṣasas. //12//

Baladeva said: "Now, as for those who disregard you with the thought, 'Who is this person of great splendor, possessing such grace and merit, other than a human body composed of the five elements?'—what will be their fate? To that, he says: 'In vain' (moghā).

Even if they are devotees of the Lord, their hope for liberation will be in vain—that is, their desire for liberation will be fruitless. If they are devoted to rituals such as the *agnihotra*, then their ritual acts will be in vain—their *agnihotra* and other rites will be mere labor."
If they were to study the Vedānta and other scriptures for the sake of knowledge, then they would possess vain knowledge—that is, their understanding of those teachings would be fruitless.
Why is this so? Because they are devoid of discernment;
the meaning is that their discriminative knowledge is obstructed by the sin born from their contempt for Me, the Supreme Brahman who is directly present within the eternal, perfected human form.
Therefore, it is stated thus in the *Bṛhad-vaiṣṇava*:
"He who considers the body of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, to be material,
should be excluded from everything according to the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti."
"Even upon merely looking at her face, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on.
If so, what fruit do they obtain?

To this he says: those who have resorted to a *prakṛti*—a nature or disposition—that is *rākṣasī*, abounding in violence and the like; *tāmasī*, belonging to the mode of ignorance; *āsurī*, belonging to the mode of passion and abounding in lust, pride, and the like; and *mohinī*, delusive and destroying discrimination—they are fit for residence in hell.
They remain. //12//
But the high-souled ones, O Pārtha, having taken refuge in my divine nature, worship me with undistracted minds, knowing me as the imperishable source of all beings. 9.13
Śrīdhara: Who, then, are those who worship you?
To this he says: "the great-souled ones" (mahātmānaḥ).
The great-souled ones are those whose minds are not overcome by desire and other such afflictions.
Therefore, those whose minds do not turn toward anything other than Me, having known Me as the imperishable cause of the world and the source of all beings, worship Me. (13)

Madhusūdana: Because those who are averse to the Blessed Lord find that their desire for fruits, the performance of obligatory, occasional, and optional rites undertaken for that purpose, and the scriptural knowledge employed for that purpose are all useless, they are devoid of both the fruits of the next world and the means to attain them. Nor do they possess any fruit of this world; for, being destitute of discriminative wisdom, they are indeed senseless.
Therefore, it has been said that all those who are excluded from all human goals are indeed to be pitied by everyone as wretched beings.

Now, it is stated who the "great-souled ones" (mahātmānaḥ) are—those who possess all human goals and are not to be pitied, being the sole refuge of the Blessed Lord. "Great" (mahān) refers to the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is the self (ātman) refined by the merits accumulated over many births and is not overcome by base desires and the like.

Those who have taken refuge in that divine and sattvic nature which will be described hereafter—beginning with "Fearlessness, purity of being," and so on—and for whom, precisely because of that, there is no mind directed toward anything else apart from Me; having known Me, the Lord, as the imperishable and undecaying cause of all beings and of the entire universe, they worship and serve Me. (13)

Viśvanātha: Therefore, those great souls who have attained greatness through the grace of my devotees acting spontaneously—even though they are human—they have attained the divine nature, the very essence of the gods; thus, while existing, they worship me in my human form alone. They are those whose minds are not directed elsewhere toward knowledge or ritual action, but are fixed on freedom from desire and the like.

"Knowing Me as the source of all beings, and that by Me all this is pervaded," and so forth—having known Me as the cause of all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, and as the imperishable because My form consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda), My devotees need only possess this much knowledge regarding My imperishability.

This very devotion, which is independent of the knowledge of the meaning of the word "thou" (tvaṃ-padārtha), ritual action, and the like, is non-dual, supreme among all, and should be regarded as the royal science and the royal secret. //13//
Baladeva: "In that case, who are those who worship You?
To this he says: "The great-souled ones.

These are those whose minds are broad and unfathomable, who know Me—the Supreme Brahman in human form—as their own essential reality, and who, through association with the virtuous, possess such devotion fixed upon Me.

Even those humans who have no liking for my form as the thousand-headed one and so forth, yet having resorted to divine nature, worship and serve me— the imperishable and eternal cause of all things such as Brahmā and Rudra— once they have known and ascertained me to be of human form.
With undivided minds, they have fixed their hearts upon me alone, even though I am manifest only in human form.
Constantly glorifying me, striving with firm vows, and bowing down to me with devotion, they worship me, ever-disciplined. (9.14)
Śrīdhara: He describes their mode of worship with two verses beginning with "constantly" (*satatam*).
Some worship and serve Me, glorifying Me at all times through hymns, mantras, and so forth, being those whose vows and observances are firm.
And striving— making an effort in the worship of the Lord and so forth, as well as in the withdrawal of the senses and other such practices—
some bow down and prostrate with devotion;
others, ever-disciplined and constantly attentive, serve [the Lord].
The terms "with devotion" and "ever-disciplined" should also be understood to apply to chanting and other such practices. //14//
Madhusūdana: It is stated in two verses how they worship [Me]. "Constantly" means at all times;

having approached a teacher established in Brahman, by means of inquiry into the statements of Vedānta during the time spent with the teacher, and at other times through the chanting of the *praṇava*, the repetition of the *Upaniṣads*, and so forth, they worship Me—the very nature of Brahman who is taught in all the *Upaniṣads*.
"Proclaiming" means making the study of the Vedānta scriptures the object of the activity of hearing; that is to say, they engage in such study.

Likewise, "firm in their vows" refers to those whose vows—non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, non-possession, and so forth—are firm, meaning they cannot be shaken by opposing forces; that is to say, they are endowed with the means of accomplishment such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-restraint (*dama*).

And so it was said by Patañjali: "Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the *yamas*. "When these are not limited by class, place, time, or occasion, and are universal, they constitute the Great Vow (*mahāvrata*). Thus, non-violence and the others are not restricted by class such as being a Brahmin, by place such as a sacred site (*tīrtha*), by time such as the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight, or by occasion such as being other than a sacrifice.

The meaning is that these [virtues], even when cultivated on the stages of the distracted, the deluded, or the occasionally distracted, are called "great vows" (mahāvrata) because they proceed in a general manner without excluding anything— such as by the resolve, "I shall not commit violence at any time, in any place, in any birth, or for any purpose such as sacrifice."
Likewise, bowing to me— paying homage to me, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the treasury of all auspicious qualities, who abides in the form of one’s chosen deity and in the form of the guru—
and by the word "and" (ca),
[including] hearing, chanting, remembering Viṣṇu, serving His feet, and so forth;
"Worship, salutation, service, friendship, and self-surrender" (BhP 7.5.23)—
by this, it should be understood that even hearing and the other limbs of devotion are to be practiced as concomitants of salutation;
furthermore, worship in the form of "service to the feet" is indeed easily accomplished toward him who is in the form of a guru.
In this context, the repetition of the word "me" (mām) is for the purpose of referring back to my qualities and form;
otherwise, it would result in redundancy.
Likewise, by the phrase "ever united with devotion"—meaning with supreme love directed toward me—it is shown that there is a perfection of all means and an absence of obstacles.
"For that high-souled one who possesses supreme devotion to the Divine, and as toward the Divine so toward the Guru, these meanings declared here indeed become manifest" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.23).
And it was stated by Patañjali: "From that [samādhi], there arises the realization of the inward-turned consciousness and the absence of obstacles" (Yoga Sūtra 1.29).

The meaning of the sūtra is that from devotion to the Lord (īśvara-praṇidhāna), there arises the attainment—that is, the direct realization—of the inward-turned consciousness whose defining characteristic is the "Thou" (tvaṃ-pada-lakṣya); furthermore, there occurs the absence of obstacles and hindrances.
Thus, those who are endowed with the means such as tranquility (śama) and self-restraint (dama), and who are devoted to the hearing and reflection upon the Vedānta, [attain this] in the Supreme Lord.
Having become free from obstacles through love for the supreme guru and by means of prostrations and other such acts, and having perfected all the necessary preparations,

these great souls worship me; they constantly contemplate me with a continuous flow of similar mental impressions (*sajātīya-pratyaya*) following upon hearing and reflection, uninterrupted by heterogeneous impressions (*vijātīya-pratyaya*).
By this, *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) is shown as the final means (*sādhana*).
When such a perfection of the means is present, that knowledge in the form of direct realization— arising from the Vedāntic texts, having the undivided [Brahman] as its object,
and consisting of the thought "I am Brahman"— is untouched by the stain of all doubts and constitutes the fruit of all the means.
By its mere arising, like a lamp, it destroys all ignorance and its effects; thus, being independent,
it is the direct cause of liberation, and not [attained] through the sequence of conquering the stages (*bhūmi*), the entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the space between the eyebrows,
the departure of the breath through the cranial channel (*brahmanāḍī*), or by way of the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi-mārga*).
It awaits either the journey to the world of Brahmā (brahma-loka) or the delay until the end of the enjoyment there.
Therefore, that which was previously promised—"I shall declare this most secret knowledge to you who are free from malice"—has now been stated.
Furthermore, its fruit, which is liberation from the inauspicious, has already been mentioned before; thus, it is not repeated here.
Thus, in this regard, this intention of the Blessed One is profound; however, its meaning when simplified is indeed manifest. //14//
Viśvanātha: It was stated that "they worship.

To the question of what that very worship consists of, he says, "constantly" (satatam) and "always" (sadā); the meaning is that here, as in the case of Karma-yoga, there is no requirement for considerations such as time, place, or the purity of the recipient.
There is no restriction of place therein, nor likewise any restriction of time.
"There is no prohibition against [uttering] the name of Śrī Hari at the beginning of impurity, O hunter," according to the Smṛti.
"Exerting themselves" means striving;
just as wretched householders strive for wealth at the doors of the rich and so forth for the sake of maintaining their families.

In the same way, my devotees strive in assemblies of devotees and other settings for the sake of attaining devotion through chanting and other such means. Having attained devotion, they practice it repeatedly, as if reading a scripture being recited;
indeed, there are so many such utterances of My names.
Those whose firm vows and observances consist of the conviction that "these many prostrations and these many services must necessarily be performed," or alternatively,
those whose firm and unbroken observances consist of vows such as the Ekādaśī fast and so forth.

The word *ca* (and) in "namasyantaś ca" is for the purpose of including all other forms of devotion not explicitly mentioned, such as hearing [My glories] and serving My feet. The term "nitya-yuktāḥ" (ever-united) uses the past participle suffix *kta* in a present sense—according to the rule that the past tense may be used for the future when expressing a desire—meaning they long for their future eternal union with Me. Thus, the meaning of the sentence is: "By glorifying Me, they indeed worship Me"; that is, the glorification of Me and so forth constitutes My worship. Therefore...
One should not suspect a tautology in the word "mām" (me). //14//
Baladeva says: He describes the modes of devotion with the two verses beginning with "constantly" (*satatam*).

"Constantly" means at all times, regardless of the purity of place, time, and so forth; they worship Me by glorifying Me—that is, by loudly uttering My names such as Govinda and Govardhanoddharaṇa, which are as sweet as nectar and connected with My auspicious qualities and deeds.
"Having gone to my temples of worship, bowing down like a staff upon the ground covered with dust and mud, and chanting my praises with devotion and an abundance of love,
they worship me"— this is the meaning of the statement that the chanting of my names and so forth is itself my worship.
Therefore, there is no tautology in the phrase "unto me."

The word *ca* (and) is a conjunctive particle that includes [other practices] not explicitly mentioned, such as hearing, worshiping, and saluting. "Exerting themselves" (*yatantaḥ*) means striving together with virtuous persons of like disposition for the sake of determining the true nature of My own form, qualities, and so forth. "Firm in their vows" (*dṛḍha-vratāḥ*) refers to those whose vows—such as fasting on Ekādaśī and Janmāṣṭamī—are firm and unswerving.

"Being ever-disciplined and desiring future constant union with Me"—here, although the action is present, the suffix *kta* (denoting the past) is used according to the rule *āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavac ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.132). //14//
And others also, sacrificing with the sacrifice of knowledge, worship me as the one,
as the distinct, and as manifold, facing in all directions. 15.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the word "knowledge" (jñāna):
the realization that Vāsudeva is everything is knowledge;
that itself is sacrifice.
While I am being worshipped by that sacrifice of knowledge, others also worship me;
therein, some do so through oneness with the realization of non-difference, while others do so through separateness with the realization of distinction, thinking, "I am your servant."
But some worship me, who am all-pervading and the self of all, in many ways as the forms of Brahmā, Rudra, and others. //15//

Madhusūdana: Now, those who are likewise unable to perform hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) as described above—being of various types, namely superior, middling, and inferior—all worship Me according to their own capacity; this He declares with the words "by the sacrifice of knowledge" (*jñāna-yajñena*).
Others, who are unable to practice the previously mentioned means, [worship] by the sacrifice of knowledge, thinking: "O Blessed One, O Divine Power, You are indeed I."

The knowledge consisting of the meditation on the identity [of the individual self with the Supreme], as stated in such Vedic texts as "I am indeed Thou," is itself a sacrifice because it takes the form of worshiping the Supreme Lord;
this is the meaning of the word "ca" (and).
The word "api" (even/also) is intended to signify the abandonment of other means.

Some, being indifferent to other means of attainment, are the most excellent ones who worship and meditate upon Me alone through the sacrifice of knowledge in the form of contemplating the non-difference between the object of worship and the worshiper, by means of oneness and the exclusion of duality.

Others, however, some who are middling, worship Me alone through the sacrifice of knowledge in the form of symbolic meditation (*pratīkopāsana*), characterized by the distinction between the object of worship and the worshiper, as stated in such scriptural passages as, "The sun is Brahman— this is the instruction" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1).

But others— some who are dull-witted and incapable of the meditation on the "I-grasping" (ahaṅgraha-upāsana) or the meditation on symbols (pratīka-upāsana), some worshipping various other deities, and others performing various rituals— worship Me alone, the Universal Form, the Self of all, in many ways through those various manifold means.
"By that respective sacrifice of knowledge" means that through the successive sequence of higher and higher [stages], there is the attainment of each preceding stage. //15//

Viśvanātha: Thus, in this chapter and in the preceding chapter, it has been shown that only the *ananya-bhakta* (the exclusive devotee) is denoted by the term "Great-Souled One" (*mahātman*), while all other types of devotees—such as those who are distressed (*ārta*) and so forth—are inferior.

He now shows those who are worshippers through identification (*ahaṅgraha-upāsaka*), worshippers of symbols (*pratīka-upāsaka*), and worshippers of the Cosmic Form (*viśvarūpa-upāsaka*) by means of the phrase "by the sacrifice of knowledge" (*jñāna-yajñena*).
The meaning is that others are not "Great-Souled Ones," being incapable of performing the previously mentioned spiritual practices.
