"Knowledge" refers to the meditation on the identity of the self (ahaṅgrahopāsana), as stated in the Śruti: "O Venerable One, I am indeed that deity, and you are indeed I," and so forth.
That itself is a "sacrifice" because it takes the form of worshiping the Supreme Lord; "by that" [is meant] by means of that.
The particle *ca* has the sense of *eva* (indeed).
The word "api" (also/even) is intended to exclude other means of accomplishment.
"As one" means by way of contemplating the non-difference between the object of worship and the worshiper.

Others, who are inferior even to that, [worship] by way of contemplating difference as distinct entities, through the worship of symbols (*pratīkopāsana*) such as the scriptural injunctions beginning with "The sun is Brahman" [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1], which constitute a sacrifice of knowledge (*jñānayajña*).

"Others, even more dull-witted than those, worship Me alone as the one whose face is everywhere, whose form is the universe, and who is the Self of all, in many ways and through many modes"— this is the explanation of the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī.

Here, according to the Tantric perspective, the worship of Gopāla that consists of the contemplation "I am Gopāla," based on the principle that "one who is not a god should not worship a god," is *ahaṅgraha-upāsanā* (worship involving identification with the deity).

Likewise, the meditation upon the single manifestation of the Lord as being distinct—thinking, "He who is the Supreme Lord Viṣṇu is indeed this Sun and none other; he is indeed Indra and none other; he is indeed Soma and none other"—is *pratīkopāsanā* (meditation on a symbol).
"Viṣṇu is all"—this is the worship of his entire majesty, which is the worship of his universal form; thus there is a threefold nature of the sacrifice of knowledge (*jñāna-yajña*).

Alternatively, through "oneness" and "separateness," there is the single worship of the *ahaṅgraha* (the identification with the deity), consisting of both types of contemplation: "I am Gopāla" and "I am the servant of Gopāla. This is like a river flowing toward the ocean, being both distinct from the ocean and non-distinct from it.
And at that time, there is a threefold classification of the sacrifice of knowledge. //15//

Baladeva: Having thus described those designated as "great souls" (mahātman) who are established solely in their own essential nature and for whom pure devotion consisting of chanting and so forth is primary, [the Lord] speaks of those devotees for whom knowledge is primary and whose chanting and so forth are subordinate, beginning with the word "knowledge" (jñāna).
Other certain devotees, distinct from the former, worship Me while sacrificing with the aforementioned sacrifice of chanting and the sacrifice of knowledge.

Regarding this, he states the manner [of worship]: they worship me—who exist in many ways, in manifold modes, as distinct entities, in the form of phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*), as the essence of *pradhāna*, *mahat*, and so forth, and with faces turned everywhere as the essence of deities such as Indra—as a unity. This is the essential point here: Kṛṣṇa, who possesses the subtle powers of consciousness and matter and whose will is true, [thought] "May I become many."

By means of His own volition, the one Lord, possessing the powers of the gross material and spiritual realms, abides in the form of the diverse universe from Brahmā down to a blade of grass; therefore, worship Me through such contemplation and by chanting My glories. //15//
I am the sacrifice; I am the oblation; I am the ancestral offering, and I am the herb.
I am the mantra; I alone am the clarified butter; I am the fire; and I am the act of offering. (9.16)
I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer, and the grandfather; I am that which is to be known, the purifier, the syllable Om, and likewise the Rig, Sama, and Yajur Vedas. //17//
He is the goal, the sustainer, the lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, and the friend;
He is the source, the dissolution, the foundation, the treasure-store, and the imperishable seed. 18.
I heat [the world], I withhold the rain and I send it forth;
I am both immortality and death, and both being and non-being, O Arjuna. 19.
Śrīdhara: He elaborates upon his nature as the Self of all with four verses beginning with "I am the sacrifice" (*kratu*).
*Kratu* refers to Vedic sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma;
*yajña* refers to Smṛti-based rites such as the five great sacrifices (*pañca-mahā-yajña*).
*Svadhā* refers to the ancestral rites such as the *śrāddha*;
*auṣadha* refers to food produced from medicinal plants or medicine itself;
and *bheṣaja* means medicine.
The mantra consists of the *yājyā*, *purodhās*, *vākya*, and so forth;
the clarified butter (*ājya*) is the means for the oblation (*homa*) and other rites;
and the fire refers to the *āhavanīya* and other sacrificial fires.
The offering and the act of sacrifice—all this is indeed myself. //16//
Furthermore,
"Father" refers to the Ordainer (Dhātṛ), the dispenser of the fruits of karma;
"the object to be known" refers to the thing that is to be cognized.
Pavitra means purifying;
or it consists of expiatory rites.
Oṃkāra is Praṇava.
The Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, are also I alone;
the rest is clear. //17//
Furthermore, as for "destination" (*gati*):
it is called a destination because it is gone to; it is the fruit (*phala*).
A "supporter" (*bhartṛ*) is one who performs the act of nourishing.
The Lord is the controller;
the witness is the observer of good and evil;
the abode is the place of enjoyment.
A refuge is a protector;
a friend is one who acts for one's welfare;
a source is that by which one comes into being preeminently, namely, a creator.
That by which something is dissolved is dissolution (pralaya), meaning the destroyer;
that in which something stands is the place (sthāna), meaning the support;
and that in which something is deposited is the receptacle (nidhāna), meaning the locus of dissolution.
The seed is the cause;
nevertheless, it is imperishable and indestructible.
The meaning is that it is not transitory like the seeds of rice and other such grains. //18//
Furthermore, regarding the statement "I heat":
abiding in the form of the sun, I heat during the summer season; that is, I cause the world to suffer heat. And at the time of rain, I release—that is, I discharge—rain.
Sometimes, however, I withhold the rain and draw it back;
immortality is life, and death is destruction;
"sat" is the gross, visible world.
And that which is non-existent and that which is subtlely visible—all this is indeed myself; having realized this, they worship me alone in many ways—this is the connection with what precedes. //19//

Madhusūdana: [Objection: If [people] worship [the Lord] in many ways, then how is it that they worship "you alone"? Anticipating this doubt, He elaborates upon His own nature as the Universal Form (viśvarūpa) in four verses, beginning with "I am. While it would have been more precise to say "I am the form of all," the mention of each individual part is made by way of a partial restatement (avayutyānuvāda), just as one speaks of the eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) and so forth when referring to the Vaiśvānara sacrifice involving twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapāla*).
*Kratu* refers to Vedic sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma.

Sacrifices refer to those prescribed by the Smṛtis, such as the Vaiśvadeva, which are renowned in the Śrutis and Smṛtis as the "great sacrifices" (mahāyajña). *Svadhā* is food being offered to the ancestors.
*Auṣadha* is food produced from medicinal herbs, or it is medicine, being consumed by all living beings.

A *mantra* is the sacrificial formula, such as the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā*, by means of which the oblation is offered to the gods. *Ājya* refers to clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and this serves as an illustration for all types of oblations.
*Agni* refers to the *āhavanīya* fire and others, which are the substrates for the casting of the oblation.
The oblation (*huta*), the act of offering (*havana*), and the casting of the sacrificial oblation (*haviṣ-prakṣepa*)—all this is indeed I, the Supreme Lord.
The word "I" is used for each individual term in order to declare that even the knowledge of each one of these constitutes the worship of the Blessed One.
The intended meaning is that there is nothing whatsoever belonging to the category of action, instrument, or result that exists apart from the Blessed One. //16//
Furthermore: he is the father, the progenitor, of this entire world and of all classes of living beings;
he is the mother, the birther;
he is the sustainer, the nourisher, or the ordainer of the respective fruits of their various actions.
The *pitāmaha* is the father of one’s father.
That which is to be known is the object to be realized (*vedya*).
That by which one is purified is the *pavitra*, the purifier—the cause of purification such as bathing in the Gaṅgā or the recitation of the Gāyatrī.
The syllable *oṃ* is the means for the realization of Brahman, which is that which is to be known;
the *ṛc* is a verse with fixed syllables and feet;
and that same verse, distinguished by its chanting, is the *sāman*.
However, the term *sāman* denotes only that which consists of chanting; this is one [type].
That which is devoid of chanting and has an indefinite number of syllables is the *yajus*.
This threefold collection of mantras is useful for ritual action.
By the word "ca" (and), the Atharva-Āṅgirasas are also included.
The word "eva" (only) serves the purpose of restriction, meaning "I alone. //17//
Furthermore, what is meant by "destination" (*gati*)? It is that which is gone toward, thus a destination; it is the fruit of action (*karma-phala*).
[These are: Brahmā, the creators of the universe, Dharma, Mahat, and the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).
The wise declare this to be the supreme, sattvic goal.
Thus, as stated by Manu and others [Manu 12.50]:
the "supporter" (bhartṛ) is the nourisher; the "giver" (dātṛ) is the one who provides the means for happiness;
the "lord" (prabhu) is the master; and the "owner" (svāmī) is the one who accepts [the child] with the thought, "This one is mine."
He is the witness who beholds the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of all living beings. He is the dwelling place because beings reside within him; it is the abode of enjoyment.
He is the refuge because suffering withers away within him; he is the remover of distress for those who have sought his protection.
A friend is one who benefits others without regard for a return favor.
*Prabhava* means origination;
*pralaya* means destruction.
*Sthāna* means the abode.
Alternatively, *prabhava* is the creator, so called because by means of it things come forth (*prakarṣeṇa bhavanti*).
*Pralaya* is the destroyer, so called because by means of it things dissolve away (*prakarṣeṇa līyante*).
"Abiding in this" means it is a place (*sthāna*), that is, a support (*ādhāra*).

"Deposited" (*nidhīyate*) means placed therein; it is a "repository" (*nidhāna*) because objects to be enjoyed at a later time are deposited in it for the purpose of enjoyment at that specific time. This refers to the substratum of all things in their subtle form, meaning the place of dissolution (*pralaya-sthāna*).
Or it is a treasure such as Śaṅkha, Padma, and so forth.
It is the seed, the cause of origination;
it is imperishable and indestructible, but not perishable like rice and other grains.
Therefore, that which is the cause—being without beginning or end—is also indeed myself; this is to be connected with what was stated previously. //18//
Furthermore, regarding the statement "I heat":
being the sun, I heat;

and consequently, by virtue of that heating, I withhold—that is, I draw up with certain rays—the rain, which is the essence (rasa) in the form of previous showers, from the earth during the eight months.
Furthermore, after four months, I release that very same restrained essence through certain rays in the form of rain and cast it upon the earth;
it is the nectar of the gods and the life-force of all living beings. The word "eva" (very/that very) is connected with the word "aham" (I).
And death is the destruction of mortals, that is, of all living beings.
That which exists in relation to something is "existent" (sat) therein;
and that which does not exist in relation to something is "non-existent" (asat) therein.
All this, O Arjuna, is indeed myself;
therefore, knowing Me as the Self of all, it is logical that you should worship Me alone in many ways according to your respective offices. //19//
Viśvanātha: Anticipating the question, "How is it that people worship You alone in so many ways?", He elaborates upon His own nature as the Universal Form (viśvarūpa) in four verses.
*Kratu* refers to Vedic sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma; *yajña* refers to Smṛti-based rites such as the Vaiśvadeva;
and *auṣadha* is food derived from medicinal herbs.
He is the Father because he produces the entire world, both individually and collectively;
he is the Mother because he sustains this world within the very midst of his own womb;
he is the Sustainer because he nourishes this world.
The Grandfather (Pitāmaha) is so called because he is the progenitor even of Brahmā, the creator of the world.
That which is to be known (vedya) is the object to be realized;
that which is purifying (pavitra) is the object that cleanses.
The destination is the fruit;
the supporter is the husband;
the master is the controller.
A witness is one who observes both the auspicious and the inauspicious;
a dwelling is a place of residence;
a refuge is a protector from calamities.
A friend is one who acts for another's benefit without any ulterior motive.
I am the creative activities such as manifestation, dissolution, and maintenance, beginning with "origination" (prabhava).
A treasure (nidhāna) refers to a storehouse of wealth, such as the Padma and Śaṅkha treasures.
The seed is the cause; it is imperishable and indestructible, but not transitory like rice and other such things. //16–18//
Becoming the sun, I scorch in the summer heat; in the rainy season, I release the rain;
and at times, in the form of a planet, I withhold the rain.
Nectar is liberation, and death is cyclic existence.

The connection with the preceding verse is as follows: "Having realized that all this—the existent and the non-existent, the gross and the subtle—is indeed Myself, worship Me, who am present everywhere. (19)
Baladeva: With four verses beginning with "I am," He demonstrates that He alone exists in the form of the universe.
*Kratu* refers to Vedic sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma;
*yajña* refers to Smṛti-based rites such as the Vaiśvadeva.
*svadhā* is that which is for the sake of the ancestors, such as the *śrāddha* and other rites; *auṣadha* is medicine, or food produced from medicinal herbs;
and *mantra* refers to the *yājyā*, *puronuvākyā*, and so forth, by means of which the oblation is offered to the gods with a specific intent.
Clarified butter (*ājya*) is the means for the oblation of ghee and so forth;
fire (*agni*) is the locus for the oblation and so forth, such as the *āhavanīya* fire;
and the offered (*huta*) is the act of oblation, the casting of the sacrificial offering (*havis*).
"I myself abide in this with my whole being; I am the father"—
thus, I alone abide here and there as the father, the mother, and the grandfather of this entire world of moving and non-moving beings.

I alone am the Ordainer (Dhātṛ), existing here and there as kings and others by virtue of being the sustainer and nourisher; for they do not differ from Me, the possessor of the powers of consciousness and matter who dwells within them as their inner controller. The object to be known—that is, the knowable thing which is pure and purifying, such as the water of the Gaṅgā and other holy waters—and the syllable *Oṃ*, which is the seed of all Vedas and the cause of knowledge regarding the knowable Brahman, as well as the *Ṛg* and other Vedas, are all I.

And the Veda is threefold; by the word "and," the Atharva [Veda] is also to be included. Among these, the *ṛc* is that which has fixed syllables in its quarters (*pāda*), while that same [verse], when distinguished by melody, is the *sāman*.
The term *sāman*, however, denotes only that which consists of chanting; this is one point.
That which is devoid of chanting and possesses immeasurable syllables is the *yajus*.
The meaning is: "I alone am this entire collection of mantras employed for ritual action, which is threefold."

*Gati* is that which consists of the goal and the means, according to the etymological definition (*nirukti*) "this is gone to" (*gam-yate*) and "by this [it is gone]" (*anayā*). *Bhartṛ* means a supporter; *pati* means a lord;
*prabhu* means a controller.
The witness (*sākṣin*) is the observer of both the auspicious and the inauspicious.

The abode (*nivāsa*) is the place of enjoyment, according to the etymology: "one dwells here. The refuge (*śaraṇa*) is the remover of the distress of those who have sought it, according to the etymology: "suffering is destroyed within this."
A friend is one who acts for one's welfare;
the sources of power and so forth are the activities of creation, dissolution, and maintenance;
and a treasure is a storehouse, such as the ninefold great lotus-treasure and others.
The seed is the cause, imperishable and indestructible; it is not perishable like rice and other such grains.
"I scorch": in the form of the sun, I myself scorch the world during the summer heat.
In the rainy season, I release the water of rain in the form of clouds; I withhold the rain and draw it back.
Amṛta is liberation (mokṣa);
mṛtyu is saṃsāra.
The existent is gross; the non-existent is subtle.
All this is indeed myself, appearing in the form of the entire world through various states of name and form in such and such diverse ways.
Others, worshipping Me through the sacrifice of knowledge with the contemplation of oneness—that Vāsudeva alone is the one omnipotent Being—adore Me. (16–19)
Those who know the three Vedas, the drinkers of Soma, purified of sin, having worshipped me with sacrifices, pray for the way to heaven.
Having attained merit, they enjoy divine celestial pleasures in heaven, in the world of the Lord of the Gods. //20//

Śrīdhara: Thus, by the two verses beginning with "The deluded disregard Me," it is shown that those who, desiring quick results, worship other deities and do not honor Me are non-devotees (*abhakta*).
By the verse beginning with "But the high-souled ones, O Pārtha," the devotees of Me (*mad-bhakta*) have been described.

Regarding this, He says in the two verses beginning with "Those who possess the three Vedas" that for those who do not worship the Supreme Lord either as one or as distinct [from the individual self], the torrent of birth and death is difficult to stem.
Those for whom the three branches of knowledge—characterized as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas—are their [study] are the *trividyāḥ*.
Those who are *trividyāḥ* are themselves the *traividyāḥ*;
here the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is used in the sense of the base word itself.
Those who study or know the three branches of knowledge are called *traividyāḥ*;
the meaning is that they are devoted to the rituals prescribed in the three Vedas.

Having worshipped me through sacrifices enjoined by the three Vedas—even though they do not know my very form as another deity, yet in reality they have worshipped and honored me alone in the form of Indra and others—[they attain their respective goals].
They are called *somapās* because they drink the *soma*, which is the remnant of the sacrifice;

being thus purified of sin and cleansed of impurity, those who pray for the heavenly path— that is, for heaven— reach and attain the celestial realm of the lord of the gods, which consists of the fruits of merit.
In heaven, in the celestial realm, they enjoy— that is, they partake of— the unsurpassed divine pleasures of the gods. //20//

Madhusūdana: Thus, those who worship the Lord in three ways—as one, as distinct, and in many forms—being free from desire, are gradually liberated by means of the purification of the mind and the arising of knowledge.
However, those who possess desires do not worship the Lord in any such manner, but rather [resort] to the means for achieving their respective desires.

They perform only those actions motivated by desire; because they lack the means for purifying their nature, they fail to ascend to the path of knowledge and thus experience nothing but the suffering of saṃsāra through the continuous cycle of birth and death again and again.
This is stated in the two verses beginning with "traividyāḥ."

Those for whom there are three branches of knowledge—the *Ṛg-veda*, *Yajur-veda*, and *Sāma-veda*—characterized respectively as the duties of the *hotṛ*, *adhvaryu*, and *udgātṛ* priests, which serve as the means for performing the ritual acts;
they are the "Tri-vidyas. By adding a suffix in its own sense (*svārthika-taddhita*), they become "Traividyas.

Alternatively, they are the performers of sacrifice (*yājñikas*) who know the three Vedas, and who, through sacrifices such as the *agniṣṭoma* and others, [perform the rites] in sequence during the three pressings (*savana*).

Having worshipped me, the formless Lord, as the Vasus and Rudras—though not knowing me in my true form—they nevertheless worship me according to the actual state of reality; and having pressed and offered the *soma*, they drink it and thus become "Soma-drinkers" (*somapa*). Being purified of sin by that very drinking of *soma*—meaning their sins, which are obstacles to the enjoyment of heaven, have been cast out—they pray for the attainment of heaven due to their possession of desire, but not [for liberation].
[This leads to] the purification of the mind, the arising of knowledge, and so forth.

Having reached the world of heaven in the celestial realm—the meritorious, meritorious-fruited, and most excellent abode of Śatakratu, the lord of the gods—they enjoy divine pleasures unattainable by humans; they partake of the desires that are the objects of enjoyment for the bodies of the gods. //20//

Viśvanātha: Even those devotees who possess these three kinds of worship are liberated only when they know Me, the Supreme Lord; however, those who are merely performers of ritual action (karmiṇaḥ) are not liberated at all. This he states in two verses beginning with "The knowers of the three Vedas" (traividyāḥ). Those who study or know the three branches of knowledge characterized by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas are the "knowers of the three Vedas" (traividyāḥ); the meaning is that they are devoted to the rituals prescribed in the three Vedas.

"Having worshipped me with sacrifices, Indra and the others—though unaware that these are indeed my own forms—have in reality worshipped me alone in the form of Indra and the rest; thus they drink the *soma*, the remnant of the sacrifice, and are therefore called *somapa*s (Soma-drinkers).

Baladeva [explains]: Having thus described the conduct of his own devotees, he speaks in the two verses beginning with "The knowers of the three Vedas" (*traividyā*) to explain their specific distinction and the conduct of those who are averse to him.
The term *trividyam* is a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) for the three branches of knowledge."
Those who study and know that [Veda] are the *traividyas*.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "one who studies that or knows that.
The meaning is: those who are devoted to the rituals prescribed in the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas.

Having worshipped Me through sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma prescribed by the three Vedas—even though Indra and the others do not know Me as My very own forms—the meaning is that they actually propitiate Me alone, who am established in those various forms.

"Soma-drinkers" refers to those who drink the Soma remaining from the sacrifice. Having become "purified of sin," meaning their impurities that obstruct the attainment of heaven and so forth have been destroyed, they pray for the path to heaven. The phrase beginning with "the merit" has a clear meaning.
The remainder [of the sentence] is "given by me alone. //20//
Having enjoyed that vast world of heaven,
they enter the world of mortals when their merit is exhausted.
Thus, those who have resorted to the dharma of the three Vedas, desiring objects of desire, obtain the state of going and returning. //21//

Śrīdhara: And then, "those [who desire heaven]"—meaning those desiring heaven, having enjoyed that vast, sought-after heavenly world and its pleasures, enter the mortal world when the merit that procured those enjoyments is exhausted.

Again, in this very same way, following the dharma prescribed by the three Vedas and desiring objects of pleasure—that is, longing for enjoyments—they obtain the state of going and returning, of coming and going. //21//

Madhusūdana says: "Then what is the undesirable [consequence]? To this he says, "They... him" (te tam). Those possessed of desire, having enjoyed that vast and extensive heavenly world obtained through their meritorious acts of longing, enter the mortal world again for the sake of taking up a body when the merit that produced those enjoyments is exhausted; thus they undergo the torments of dwelling in the womb and so forth once more.
The meaning is "they experience.
"Again and again" means in the manner already described.
The particle *hi* is used for the purpose of indicating what is well-known.
*Traidharmyam* refers to the threefold duty consisting of the duties of the *hotṛ*, *adhvaryu*, and *udgātṛ* priests; it denotes optional rites such as the *jyotiṣṭoma* and others.
Even when the reading is *trayī-dharmam*, the meaning remains the same: the duty (*dharma*) propounded by the *trayī*, that is, by the three Vedas.
The prefix *anu-* is used because these rites depend upon prior understandings within the beginningless cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*).
Immediately after their previous practice, they return to the world of humans and practice once again.
Desiring desires—that is, longing for divine enjoyments—they thus obtain the cycle of going and coming. Having performed karma, they go to heaven; returning from there, they perform karma again.
The intention is that the continuous stream of torments, such as dwelling in the womb, thus pursues them incessantly. //21//
Viśvanātha: Coming and going again and again—death and birth. //21//

Baladeva said: And then, "those" refers to those seekers of heaven who, having enjoyed that requested heavenly world, enter the mortal world when the merit that brought them there has been exhausted; they obtain births as Brahmins and others on earth according to the method described in the Pañcāgni-vidyā, and once again, performing the dharma ordained by the three Vedas in exactly this same way.
Those who desire sense-objects, longing for the enjoyments of heaven, obtain the state of going and returning; that is to say, they transmigrate. //21//
For those people who worship Me, thinking of no other, and who are constantly devoted to Me— for them, I provide for their acquisition and preservation. 9.22

Śrīdhara: He says "ananyāḥ" (those who have no other) to show that my devotees, by my grace, become successful in their purpose. "Ananyāḥ" means those for whom there is nothing else to desire apart from me.

Those people who, being such, serve me while meditating upon me—for them, who are constantly engaged and always devoted to me alone—I provide *yoga* (the acquisition of wealth and so forth), *kṣema* (the preservation thereof), and *mokṣa* (liberation).
Or rather, even if they do not request it, I myself carry them; that is, I cause them to reach their destination. //22//
Madhusūdana explains: "But those who are free from desire and possess perfect vision are 'non-dual' (ananya).
Those for whom no other object exists as a focus of dualistic perception are "non-dual"—that is, perceivers of universal non-duality who are devoid of longing for any enjoyment.
Having realized: "I alone am the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the Self of all; there is nothing whatsoever apart from Me," they worship Him.

Thus, those people who—being endowed with the fourfold means and being renunciants (saṃnyāsins)—constantly contemplate Me, Nārāyaṇa, as the Inner Controller (ātmatvena), and perceive Me everywhere without limitation, they, through non-difference from Me, have indeed accomplished all that was to be done; this is the implied meaning.

For those who are established in the vision of non-duality and are utterly free from desire, how can there be the acquisition and preservation (yoga-kṣema) of anything, since they themselves make no effort?

To address this, he says: "I bring about both *yoga* and *kṣema* for those who are constantly engaged [in yoga], who are perpetually and tirelessly occupied with meditation with devotion, and who do not even strive for the mere maintenance of their bodies— those who,
though desiring neither *yoga* (the acquisition of the unobtained) nor *kṣema* (the preservation of what has been obtained), I, the Lord of All, carry and deliver."
Among them, the one who possesses knowledge, who is constantly disciplined, and who is single-mindedly devoted, is preeminent;
for I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge, and he is dear to Me.
Thus it has been said in [Gītā 7.17]:

"Although the Blessed One carries the acquisition and preservation (yoga-kṣema) of all beings alike, nevertheless there is a distinction: for others He carries it by instigating effort, whereas for the wise He carries it without instigating effort for that purpose. //22//

Viśvanātha: [The Lord] says "the others" (*ananye*) to show that for those who are exclusively devoted to Him, happiness is not obtained through ritual action (*karma*), but is indeed granted by Him alone. "Of the wise who are always and ever intent" means that others are perpetually unwise;
or else, it refers to those who desire constant union—where "union" (*yoga*) is the acquisition of wealth and so forth, and "security" (*kṣema*) is its preservation. By those various [means],...

The meaning is this: even though it is not required [of them], one carries and acts [for them] thinking "I alone carry and I act"; by employing the expression "I carry," the burden of nourishing their bodies is borne by me alone, just as the burden of nourishing one's own wife, children, and so forth is borne by a householder.

Nor should it be said that, like others, even their acquisition and preservation (yoga-kṣema) are to be attained through action; for what need have you, the Supreme Lord who delights in the Self and is indifferent in every respect, for carrying that burden?
Devotion is worshiping Him; that is the fixing of the mind upon Him here and now, free from the conditions of this world or the next. This alone is *naiṣkarmya* (freedom from action).
According to the Śruti, because My other devotees possess *naiṣkarmya* through their desirelessness, the happiness seen in them is given by Me alone.
In this regard, it should be understood that even though I am indifferent toward all else, my sole motive is affection for my own devotees.
Nor should it be said that those devotees who place the burden of their own salvation upon you, their chosen deity, are devoid of love;
for they have not surrendered the burden of their own responsibility to me at all, but rather I have accepted it by my own will.
Furthermore, this burden of creating the universe and so forth should not be understood as a heavy task for me performed by mere volition;

rather, for me who am attached to my devotees, carrying their welfare and security (yoga-kṣema) is like carrying the weight of a beloved wife who is one's own object of enjoyment—it is exceedingly blissful. //22//
Baladeva: Now, he specifically describes His own devotees with the words "those who are undivided" (*ananya*).

Those persons who are *ananya*—having Me alone as their sole purpose—who worship and serve Me by meditating upon and contemplating Me as the abode of the jewels of auspicious qualities, as the source of the nectar of diverse and wonderful pastimes, and as the locus of divine manifestations; for them...

For those who are constantly and at all times devoted to Me, having forgotten the maintenance of their own bodies, I alone carry their *yoga-kṣema*— that is, the acquisition of food and its preservation.

By using the word "carry" (*vahāmi*) rather than saying "I do it," it is indicated that the burden of nourishing them must be borne by Me alone, just as the burden of supporting a family is borne by the householder.

Thus says the author of the Sūtra: "Because the fruit is declared for the master; so says Ātreya" (VS 3.4.44). Regarding this, they say: "For those who constantly desire application together with me toward the yoga characterized by attaining Me and the security characterized by non-return from Me, I Myself carry that burden; the task of leading them to Me is Mine alone."
But this does not apply to the host of deities beginning with the Radiant One (arcis).
He will explain this very point in the twelfth chapter with the two verses beginning "But those who [perform] all actions," and so forth.
The author of the Sūtras also says this and shows the distinction: "And he shows the distinction" (VS 4.3.16). //22//
Even those who, devoted to other deities, worship them endowed with faith— they too, O son of Kuntī, worship me alone, though not according to the prescribed rule.
Śrīdhara: But surely, since in reality there is no other deity apart from You, even those who serve Indra and the other gods are indeed Your devotees; so how could they undergo coming and going?
To this he says, "Even those...

Being endowed with faith and being devotees, it is true that those people who worship other deities in the form of Indra and others, they too worship Me alone—but it is without following the prescribed injunctions (*avidhi-pūrvakam*).
They sacrifice without the procedure that leads to liberation;
therefore, they return again. //23//
Madhusūdana: But surely, you alone are all other deities as well, because there is no other entity distinct from you.
Thus, even those who worship other deities are actually worshipping you alone; therefore, there would be no distinction at all.
Consequently, those who desire objects of desire—such as the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, and others—attain only the state of going and returning.
To the question, "How is it said that those who think of no other [deity] have already accomplished their duty? He says, "Even those...

Just as My devotees worship Me alone, so too those who are devotees of other deities—such as the Vasus and others—and who worship them with sacrifices like the Jyotiṣṭoma, endowed with faith and a sense of conviction, they too, O Kaunteya, like My own devotees, worship and honor Me alone, who abide in the form of those respective deities.

"According to improper rites" means preceded by "improperity," which is ignorance; the meaning is that, having failed to know Me as the Self of all and having conceptualized objects and so forth as distinct from Me, they sacrifice. //23//
Viśvanātha: Now, by the statement "and others [worship] by the sacrifice of knowledge" (*jñāna-yajñena*), you yourself have described three types of worship.
Among those, the third type of worship was indicated by the phrase "the one whose face is everywhere" (*viśvato-mukham*).
Furthermore, through the passage beginning with "I am the ritual (*kratu*), I am the sacrifice (*yajña*)," the fact that you possess a universal form (*viśva-rūpatva*) has been demonstrated.
Therefore, those who perform sacrifices to Indra and other deities as part of the ritual action (*karma-yoga*), as well as those who are primarily devoted to other deities, are indeed Your devotees.
How is it, then, that they are not liberated?
As You have stated: "Those who desire objects of desire attain the state of going and returning."
"But their fruit is finite," it is said;

regarding this, he says, "Even those who worship Me alone"—this is true—but they worship without the prescribed rule, that is, without the ritual injunction that leads to Me; therefore, they return again. //23//

Baladeva: If it is asked, "But surely even those who sacrifice to Indra and others are in reality sacrificing to You alone; why then do they experience coming and going?"—to that he says, "Even those...

Those people who are devotees of other deities, possessing devotion toward Indra and others alone, and being endowed with faith—and therefore with firm conviction that [those gods] are the bestowers of results—sacrifice with rituals, meaning they worship them.
It is true that they also worship me alone;
however, they worship me without following the prescribed rule—that rule by which, through my attainment, there would be a cessation of coming and going.
Therefore, they obtain only that [result]. //23//
For I alone am the enjoyer and also the Lord of all sacrifices; yet they do not recognize Me in truth, and therefore they fall. 24.
Śrīdhara explains this very point with the words "I am":
I alone am the enjoyer and the lord— the master— of all sacrifices, appearing in the form of their respective deities.
The meaning is: "I alone am also the giver of the fruit.
They do not recognize me, who am such, in truth and as I truly am;
therefore they fall away, they perish, and they return again.
But those who, seeing me alone as the inner controller within all the deities, worship them, do not return [to this world]. //24//

Madhusūdana, explaining how [the sacrifice] is performed contrary to the prescribed rules (*avidhi-pūrvakatva*), states that these [sacrificers] fall from their fruits with the words "I indeed" (*ahaṃ hi*).

I, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, am the enjoyer of all sacrifices—both those prescribed by the Vedas (*śrauta*) and those based on tradition (*smārta*)—in the form of their respective deities; and because I am the presiding deity (*adhiyajña*) through my own nature as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), it is well known that I am also the Master and the bestower of the fruit.

But those who sacrifice to other deities do not know me in this way— that is, in truth, as the enjoyer and the sovereign Lord Vāsudeva alone, who, in the form of the sacrificial materials and so forth, is the enjoyer of sacrifices, and in his own essential form, is the giver of their fruits; they do not know that there is no other object of worship besides him.

Therefore, due to a lack of full knowledge of my true nature, even after performing sacrifices with great effort, those who have not dedicated their actions to me go by the path of smoke and so forth to the various worlds of the gods; at the end of those enjoyments, they fall away—meaning they descend—from those worlds because the karma that produced those enjoyments is exhausted.
Separated from those bodies and the like, they return to the world of men to take up another body once again.

However, those who worship while perceiving the Blessed Lord alone as the inner controller within each respective deity, having offered their actions to the Blessed Lord, go to the world of Brahman by way of the path beginning with light (arcir-ādi) through the power of those actions accompanied by that knowledge; there, having attained right vision, they are liberated at the conclusion of those enjoyments—this is the distinction. //24//
Viśvanātha: He states the very fact of acting contrary to injunction with the words "I am.
[He means: "I alone am the enjoyer, the Lord, the Master, and the giver of the fruit, appearing in the form of other deities;
yet they do not know Me in truth."
Just as I am a devotee of Sūrya,
may Sūrya alone be gracious toward me;
may Sūrya alone grant me my desired fruit.
Their understanding is that the sun alone is the Supreme Lord;
however, it is not that the Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa himself is the sun,
but rather that he is the one who generates such faith in them.
"He alone is the one who bestows upon me the fruit of the worship of the Sun"—
those who are devoted with such a notion fall away from reality because they lack true knowledge of Me.

However, those who worship Me, whose face is turned toward all directions, with the realization that "the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa alone is being propitiated in the form of the Sun and others," are indeed liberated.

Therefore, it is indicated that worship directed toward My manifestations, such as the sun and others, must be performed preceded by knowledge of My manifestations; it should not be done otherwise. //24//
Baladeva explains the lack of accordance with the prescribed rule: "I indeed... and so forth.
They do not recognize Me in truth as I am—the one who, in the form of Indra and others, am the enjoyer, the lord, the master, the protector, and the bestower of fruits of all sacrifices;
therefore, they fall away and transmigrate. //24//

Those who are devoted to the gods go to the gods; those who are devoted to the ancestors go to the ancestors; those who worship the spirits go to the spirits; and those who sacrifice to me go to me. (9.25)
Śrīdhara explains that very point with the words "they go" (yānti):
those whose vow—that is, their observance—is directed toward the gods, such as Indra and others, go to the gods;
therefore, they return again.

Those whose vow is toward the ancestors—those intent on rites such as the *śrāddha*—go to the ancestors. Those for whom worship (*ijyā*) consists of offerings to spirits (*bhūta*), such as the *vināyaka*s and *mātṛ*s, are "worshippers of spirits" (*bhūtejyā*); they go to the spirits. Those whose habit is to sacrifice to me are "my worshippers" (*mad-yājinaḥ*).
They go to me alone, who am imperishable and whose very nature is supreme bliss. //25//

Madhusūdana: Although those who worship other deities do not obtain the fruit of non-return, it is certain that they obtain corresponding minor fruits from each respective deity; stating this, [the Lord] says "they go" (*yānti*) to express the distinction of those who worship the Blessed One from them.

For those who worship without following the prescribed injunctions are of three kinds, due to the division of the three qualities (*guṇa*) of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) which is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Among them, those characterized by *sattva* are devoted to the gods (*deva-vrata*).

The gods are Vasu, Rudra, Āditya, and so forth; those whose vow consists of worship—taking the form of offerings, oblations, circumambulation, prostration, and the like—are connected to them. According to the Vedic scripture, "As one worships, so one becomes," they go to those very gods.
Those characterized by passion (*rājasas*), however, being devoted to the ancestors, worship the *pitaras* such as the Agniṣvāttas through rites like the *śrāddha*; they go to those very ancestors.

Likewise, those characterized by darkness (*tāmasas*) perform sacrifices to elemental spirits (*bhūtejyā*); they worship spirits such as Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Vināyakas, and the hosts of Mothers, and they go to those very spirits.

Here, the words "deity," "ancestor," and "spirit" are used in a compound with the *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) of their respective associates, according to the maxim of the "camel-faced" (*uṣṭramukha*).

Because the elision of the middle term (*madhyama-pada-lopa*) in a compound is not accepted here, and because the fourth-case compound expressing "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya-caturthī-samāsa*) is impossible due to the absence of a relationship between an original material and its transformation (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*),
and because the word *jyā*— which signifies worship— is employed at the end [of the verse], the word *vrata* in the first two instances must also refer exclusively to worship.

Thus, having stated that the propitiation of other deities results in a finite fruit consisting of becoming the very form of those respective deities, [the text now speaks] of the propitiation of the Blessed Lord.

He describes the infinite fruit, which is the state of having the Lord's own form: those whose nature it is to sacrifice to and worship Me, the Blessed One, are "My sacrificers" (mad-yājinaḥ); perceiving the nature of the Blessed One in all deities and being solely intent on propitiating the Blessed One, they go to Me alone, the Blessed One.

The intention is this: "Alas, how great is the power of the misfortune of the ignorant! For while the effort is equal, they fail to propitiate the Blessed One—who is without interval [in granting results] and who bestows infinite fruit—and instead, by propitiating another deity, they obtain only limited results. (25)
Viśvanātha: Now, it may be argued that whatever procedure is prescribed in the manual for the worship of a particular deity, that very deity is indeed worshipped according to that procedure;
just as Vaiṣṇavas worship Viṣṇu using the very procedure found in the manual for the worship of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, if one asks what fault there is for those devoted to other deities, [the answer is] true.
"In that case, it is simply a matter of logic that the devotees of each respective deity surely attain that very deity," [the Lord] says with the words "they go" (yānti).

Since those various deities themselves are perishable, how can the devotees of those various deities become imperishable? However, I am imperishable and eternal; therefore, it is indicated that my devotees are also imperishable, and thus they are indeed eternal.
"You alone remain, known as Śeṣa" (BhP 10.3.25);
"Nārāyaṇa alone existed, neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara";
"At the end of a parārdha, he awoke; he appeared before me in the form of a cowherd" (GTU 1.25).
And my devotees do not fall away even during the great dissolution, according to such scriptural and traditional texts as [the Skanda Purāṇa, Kāśī-khaṇḍa]. //25//
Baladeva: In reality, although I exist in the form of those various deities and so forth, they do not attain Me simply because they lack knowledge of Me in that form; thus He says, "They go.
Here, in the first verse-quarter, the word *vrata* denotes worship, as is evident from the word *ijyā* in the subsequent verse-quarter.
Those who have the gods as their *vrata*—the worshippers of the gods—who sacrifice to Indra and others through Sāttvika rites such as the *darśa* and *paurṇamāsa*, go to them alone.
Those of rajasic nature, devoted to the ancestors, worship the ancestors through rites such as the *śrāddha* and go to them alone.

Those of tamasic nature, who worship spirits, propitiate yakṣas, rakṣasas, and vināyakas with various offerings of oblations and go to those very beings. But those who sacrifice to Me—being free from the qualities—worship Me with easily obtained materials and go to Me alone.
The word *api* is used in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).

This is the meaning: "We are the worshippers of Indra and the others; they alone are our lords, who, being pleased by our offerings, will grant us the fruits we desire"—such is the conception of those who serve deities other than Me.
[In contrast,] Vāsudeva, who possesses all powers and is the Lord of all, exists in the form of those very deities and so forth.
"The thought of my servants is this: 'Our Lord, being propitiated by rituals that are easy to perform, will grant all our desires.

Consequently, even though they perform the very same rituals as those who serve the gods and other deities, because they are averse to the contemplation of Me, they obtain only their own [worldly] desires—which are short-lived and of little power—and having enjoyed limited pleasures along with them,"
Upon their destruction, they perish;

but those who serve Me—having attained Me, the Lord of All, who am without beginning or end, whose resolve is ever-true, whose glory is infinite, who consists of consciousness and bliss, and who am affectionate toward My devotees—do not return from Me again, but instead enjoy endless joys with Me, sporting in My divine abode. //25//
"Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water— that offering presented with devotion by one of purified self, I accept. (BhG 9.26)
Śrīdhara: Thus, the imperishable fruit for one's own devotees has been stated. Furthermore, he demonstrates the effortless nature of devotion to himself with the words "a leaf" (patram).
To him who offers even a mere leaf, flower, or the like to me with devotion—that is, with love—even if his mind is not disciplined, [I accept it].
I eat that leaf, flower, and so forth, offered with devotion by one of pure mind and desireless bhakti who has presented it to Me.
Indeed, for Me, the Supreme Lord and Master of great opulence, there can be no satisfaction through rituals involving yoga and the like that require vast wealth— as is the case with minor deities—
but rather through devotion alone.
Therefore, the intended meaning is: "Whatever little, even just a leaf or the like, is offered by a devotee, I eat that solely for the sake of bestowing grace upon them. //26//

Madhusūdana: Thus, having set aside other deities, one should worship the Blessed Lord alone because His worship yields infinite fruit and is exceedingly easy to perform; this is what He says with the words "A leaf" (patram).

Whatever object—a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, or anything else obtained without effort—any person whatsoever may offer with devotion to Me, the Supreme Lord, the Master of infinite and great manifestations, [knowing] that there is nothing higher than Vāsudeva.

With a love preceded by the thought "Does he have anything?", he offers to the Lord like a servant; for since there is no object in the world that does not fall within my ownership— because everything has been acquired by me alone—
the person offers back to me everything that is indeed mine.
When one who is self-restrained and pure in intellect offers even a trivial object such as a leaf or a flower with love, I—the Lord of all—eat it; that is, I accept it with love as if eating.
Here, by the extreme disparagement of the word "eating" (aśana), a specific mode of acceptance characterized by "eating" is revealed as the cause of an excess of love.
Indeed, the gods neither eat nor drink; this alone is their nectar.
For it is heard in the scriptures that "they are satisfied by merely seeing [it].
Why, then, do you eat even that which is trivial?
Because it has been "offered with devotion"—that is, surrendered with love; the meaning is that this surrender out of love is for the purpose of my acceptance.

Having stated here that one should offer "with devotion," He further says "offered with devotion" (*bhakty-upahṛtam*) to indicate an exclusive restriction (*parisaṅkhyā*): that for one who lacks devotion, being a Brāhmaṇa, asceticism, or other such qualities, do not constitute grounds for My acceptance.

Like a child whose knowledge of what is fit or unfit to eat is bound by a particular affection and who eats rice grains brought by the Śrīdāma Brāhmaṇa, or like a child who eats leaves, flowers, and so forth offered by his mother and others, [I accept] what is offered by a devotee.
Or [he might think], "I shall consume [Him] directly.

By this, the intention is that devotion alone is the cause of my satisfaction, and not some offering of oblations (*bali*) or gifts as in the case of other deities, which must be accomplished through the expenditure of much wealth and effort; thus, setting aside other deities, one should worship Me alone. //26//
Viśvanātha: [The Lord] says "the leaf" (patram) to show that the greater exertion involved in devotion to another deity is preferable [only in comparison], but not so in the case of devotion to Me.
Here, "bhaktyā" functions as the instrumental case (*karaṇa*).
If it were used in the locative (*tṛtīyā* [as *bhaktau*]), there would be the redundancy of saying "offered with devotion" (*bhakty-upahṛtam*).
Therefore, the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment;
the meaning is "those accompanied by devotion" (*bhaktyā sahitaḥ*), i.e., my devotees (*mad-bhaktāḥ*).
By this, it is indicated that I do not eat at all—even if it is offered by him—any leaf, flower, or the like, which a person other than my devotee gives out of a temporary or momentary devotion.
And therefore, whatever—such as leaves and so forth—a devotee of Mine gives, that I eat; I consume it in the proper manner.
Of what kind? It means: offered with devotion, and not given out of consideration for anyone else or for any other reason.

Furthermore, He says "I do not eat" even when My devotee possesses an impure body, by specifying "of one whose self is restrained" (*prayatātmanaḥ*), meaning one whose body is pure; thus those such as women in their menses are excluded.
Alternatively, "of one whose self is restrained" means one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is pure; for there is no one other than My devotee who possesses a pure internal organ.
A person whose self is washed [pure] [attains] the foot-base of Kṛṣṇa.
From the statement of Parīkṣit, "He does not let go" (BhP 2.8.5), it is clear that the very inability to abandon service to My feet is the mark of a pure heart.
Therefore, even if desire, anger, and so forth should occasionally arise, they should be understood as being ineffective—like the bite of a snake whose fangs have been pulled out. //26//

Baladeva: Having stated that devotion to Me should be practiced because it yields inexhaustible and infinite fruit, He says "A leaf" (patram) to show that it should also be practiced because it is easily accomplished.
Whosoever offers with devotion—that is, with an abundance of love—a leaf, a flower, or whatever other thing is easily available, to Me, the Lord of All; [I accept that gift].
Whatever is offered with devotion and presented with love by him, I—possessing infinite opulences and having all desires fulfilled—eat; that is, I enjoy it as is appropriate.
Or rather, having hunger and thirst aroused by affection for him, I eat all of that through being absorbed in devotion to him.
To the question "Of what kind of person? he says: "of one whose self is restrained," meaning one whose mind is purified and who is free from desire.
Thus it has been said: "I eat that which is offered by one who is free from desire and devoted to me; however, I do not eat what is offered by one whose disposition is the opposite.
Although it was already stated "with devotion," the further statement "offered with devotion" is made to emphasize that devotion alone is what pleases me.
However, he indicates that this is not [attained] through divine status or asceticism.

Here, the pure devotion consisting of chanting and so forth— described by the three verses beginning with "Always single-mindedly as a leaf"— must be performed as something already offered (*arpitā*), and not as something offered after having been performed (*kṛtvārpitā*).

Thus, from the words of Prahlāda: "If devotion characterized by the ninefold marks, offered by a person to Viṣṇu, is truly performed toward the Blessed Lord, I consider that to be the highest study. (BhP 7.5.19)
Therefore, it is not stated thus here. //26//
Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give away, and whatever austerity you practice, O son of Kuntī, perform that as an offering unto Me. 27.
Śrīdhara: Nor should even leaves, flowers, and so forth be acquired through efforts for my sake alone and offered up, like the animals, Soma, and other materials used for sacrifice.
What then? "Whatever you do" refers to whatever action you perform, whether by nature or according to scripture;
likewise, "whatever you eat."
Whatever you offer as an oblation, whatever you give as a gift, and whatever austerity you practice— whatever penance you perform.
Act in such a way that all of this is indeed offered unto me. //27//
Madhusūdana: [The Lord] describes what kind of devotion yours is in the verse beginning with "whatever you do" (*yat karoṣi*).
Whatever you do—even apart from the scriptures—such as walking and so forth, which is prompted by passion; whatever you eat for your own satisfaction or for the success of your undertakings;
and likewise, whatever oblation you offer, such as the daily *agnihotra* sacrifice and others, which you perform by the authority of the scriptures.
This is an indication of all oblations prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti.
Likewise, whatever food, gold, and so forth you give to guests, Brahmins, and others;

likewise, whatever austerity you perform—such as the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances every year for the removal of unknown or inadvertent sins—and whatever you do to restrain unrestrained activity, [directing] the aggregate of the body and senses...
Or [the phrase] "you restrain" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) duties. By this,
it refers to those activities such as walking or eating which necessarily occur for you by the very nature of living beings, even without the guidance of the scriptures.

And whatever acts such as fire-offerings (homa) and giving (dāna), which are necessarily required by the authority of the scriptures— O Kaunteya, perform all that, whether worldly or Vedic, being performed for some other motive, in such a way that it becomes "offered unto Me" (mad-arpaṇam), meaning it is dedicated to Me.
By the use of the middle voice (ātmanepada), He shows that the fruit of the dedication resides solely in the one who dedicates, and not that anything at all accrues to Me.
The intention is this: the dedication of inevitable karmas unto Me, the Supreme Guru, is itself devotion to Me; no separate activity need be performed for that purpose. //27//

Viśvanātha: Now, with the expectation— "Among these various types of devotion you have described, beginning with 'the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise,' which one indeed should I practice?"—

O Arjuna, for the time being, since it is impossible for you to abandon action, knowledge, and so forth, you have no qualification for the exclusively supreme and undivided devotion (*ananya-bhakti*), nor for the inferior devotion characterized by desire (*sakāma-bhakti*).
Therefore, He says in two verses beginning with "Whatever you do" that you should practice devotion alone as the primary focus, which is free from desire and conjoined with action and knowledge:
"Whatever work you do— whether worldly or Vedic—
and whatever you eat, such as food and drink in the course of daily life, and whatever austerity you perform— all that you should do as an offering unto Me alone."
Nor should it be said that this is exclusively the yoga of selfless action (niṣkāma-karma-yoga) and not the yoga of devotion (bhakti-yoga);
for by those performing selfless action, the very action prescribed by the scriptures is offered unto the Blessed Lord.
But nothing at all has been done on the conventional level, for that is how it is observed everywhere.
Devotees, however, offer only the activities of their own body, mind, vital breaths, and senses to the Blessed Lord, their chosen deity.
As it was stated in the very section on devotion (bhakti-prakaraṇa): "Whether by body, speech, mind, senses, intellect, or self, because one follows their respective natures..."
"Whatever one does entirely,
one should offer that to Nārāyaṇa. Now,
it may be argued that this act of offering, expressed by "you sacrifice," is merely a subordinate limb of worship and devotion, intended solely for Viṣṇu.
"You are performing austerity.
But this austerity is indeed in the form of vows such as those of Ekādaśī;
therefore, why is this not called nothing other than devotion itself?
Indeed, truth is that devotion which, even if performed, is not offered to the Lord; rather, it is known as such only when it is actually offered to the Lord.
As it was said by Śrī Prahlāda regarding the verse beginning with "Hearing, chanting, and remembering Viṣṇu": "Thus [the service] is offered by a person."
Regarding the passage, "If devotion to Viṣṇu is to be practiced with its nine characteristics" (BhP 7.5.18–19), the commentary by the venerable Śrī Svāmī-carapaṇas states:
"Devotion is performed toward the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu; and that [devotion], provided it is indeed offered [to Him], if it is thus practiced..."
But since it is not the case that [the meaning] is handed over after having been already produced, this verse does not conclude with the mere [word]. //27//
Baladeva: By the words beginning with "constantly" (*satatam*), I have declared to you the devotion of those who are independent [of worldly motives].

However, you, being one who has attained perfection, even while performing devotional acts such as chanting (*kīrtana*), must also practice devotion toward Me by surrendering all actions for the sake of the welfare of the world; with this intention, He says:
"That which..."—namely, that worldly action which you perform to sustain the maintenance of the body.
And that food and so forth which you eat for the sake of maintaining the body;
likewise, that which you offer as oblations, performing Vedic sacrifices such as the Agnihotra; and that food, gold, and other gifts which you give to worthy recipients—[all this is offered to Me].
Every year, you perform the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances for the destruction of unknown sins;
perform all of that in such a way that it may be an offering unto Me.
By that, through the gathering of this world for My sake, My great grace shall come to pass upon you.
Nor should it be said that this devotion, consisting of the surrender of all actions, belongs only to those who possess firm realization (*sa-niṣṭha*);
for by them, only Vedic rites are surrendered therein. Rather, this belongs exclusively to those who are fully perfected (*pariniṣṭhita*).
Because, by the Lord’s instruction beginning with "Whatever you do," all actions are offered unto Him;
for they, desiring to remove the effort required for the Lord's maintenance of the world, perform those actions in such a way that they please Him. //27//

Thus, you shall be liberated from the bonds of action, which yield both auspicious and inauspicious fruits; with your self disciplined by the yoga of renunciation, being fully released, you shall come unto Me. 28.

Śrīdhara: And so, hear what fruit you will obtain: "By performing thus... By acting in this way, you will be liberated from the bonds of action—namely, the desirable and undesirable fruits caused by action—because, since all actions have been surrendered to Me, it is impossible for you to have any connection with their results; and being thus liberated from them...
"One whose self is disciplined by the yoga of renunciation": renunciation is the offering of actions unto Me;
that itself is yoga.
One whose mind (ātman) is joined with that [is "one whose self is disciplined by the yoga of renunciation"].
Having become such, you shall attain me. //28//
Madhusūdana: He states the fruit of such worship in the verse beginning with "śubhāśubha.

Even though my worship, consisting of the surrender of all actions, is thus accomplished without effort, you shall be liberated from those bonds of action—which are of the nature of bondage and consist of actions whose fruits are auspicious and inauspicious, desired and undesired—because they have been surrendered unto Me.
Because that connection [with action] is impossible for you, you shall not be bound by actions and their fruits.
Consequently, one whose self—the internal organ—is joined with the yoga of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-yoga*): *saṃnyāsa* is the surrendering of all actions to the Blessed Lord;
it is like *yoga* because it purifies the mind, and thus it is called *yoga*. One whose self is "joined" (*yukta*) with that—that is, whose internal organ has been purified—[is as described].

Whether you have renounced all actions or, while still living, are liberated from the bonds of action, you shall attain Me through right vision by the cessation of the veil of ignorance— that is, you will realize "I am Brahman.
Then, upon the exhaustion of the *prārabdha* karma and the falling away of this body, you shall attain Me in the form of disembodied liberation (*videha-kaivalya*).

The meaning is that even now, though possessing My form, you shall not become an object of conventional discourse regarding illusory difference through the cessation of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi). //28//
Viśvanātha: You shall be liberated from the bonds consisting of endless karmic forms, which yield both auspicious and inauspicious fruits.
Devotion (*bhakti*) is the worship of Him;
it is the mental conceptualization of Him alone, through the absence of any limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) pertaining to this world or the next.
And this very state is "freedom from action" (*naiṣkarmya*), according to the scripture [GTU 1.14].
Renunciation is the abandonment of the fruits of action; he whose self—that is, whose mind—is joined with that is one who possesses yoga.
Not only will you become liberated, but being even more distinguished than those already liberated, you shall attain Me—you shall come into My presence to serve Me directly.
Even among the liberated and the perfected ones, O great sage, one who is devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa and possesses a tranquil mind is extremely rare, even among tens of millions.
This is according to the traditional teaching (smṛti):

"He bestows liberation at some time, but never the yoga of devotion" (BhP 5.6.18), as stated by Śuka. The underlying meaning is that this very service of love for Me is superior even to liberation itself. //28//
Baladeva says: He states the fruit of such devotion with the words "by auspicious...
When devotion—characterized by the surrender of all actions performed according to My direction—is thus established, you shall be liberated from the bonds consisting of karma.

To the question "of what kind?", he replies: "by auspicious... meaning by those [bonds] which consist of desired and undesired fruits, which oppose the attainment of that [liberation], and which are ancient.
To the question "What kind of person are you?", he says: "Sannyāsa" is the dedication of actions unto Me;
that very act is "yoga" because it purifies the mind, and one whose self—that is, the mind—is endowed with that is "yukta-ātmā.
Not only will you be liberated from actions, but being fully liberated, you shall come to Me.
Being distinguished among the liberated, you shall come into my presence to serve me directly. //28//
I am equal toward all beings; to Me there is none hateful and none dear.
But those who worship Me with devotion, they are in Me, and I too am in them. 29.
Śrīdhara: If you grant liberation only to devotees and not to non-devotees, do you then possess partiality caused by attachment, aversion, and so forth? He says "no" with the words, "I am equal.
"I am equal toward all beings."
Therefore, for me there is indeed neither one who is dear nor one who is hateful.
Even so, those who devote themselves to me are my devotees and abide in me;
I too abide in them as their benefactor.
The meaning is this: just as fire, even while dispelling the sufferings of darkness, cold, and so forth for those very close to it, incurs no partiality;
or just as the wish-fulfilling tree [does not];
in the same way, there is indeed no partiality on my part, even though I am partial toward my devotees.
But this greatness belongs solely to my devotion. //29//

Madhusūdana: [Objection: "If you favor only devotees and not non-devotees, then how can you be the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) given that you possess attachment and aversion? To this he says, "I am equal" (*samo'ham*).

I am equal—that is, identical—toward all living beings by virtue of my being the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), which is natural and not adventitious, and which consists of existence (*sat*), consciousness (*cit*), and bliss (*ānanda*).
Therefore, for Me—who am like the light of the sun pervading the entire circle of the sky—there exists no object of hatred nor any object of affection.

If that is so, how is it that there is a disparity in the results for the devotee and the non-devotee? To this He replies: "But those who worship Me"—that is, those who serve Me through devotion consisting of the surrender of all actions.
The word "but" (*tu*) is used to highlight the distinction of the devotees in comparison with the non-devotees.

Who is that [I]? They are those whose internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) have been purified by actions performed without desire and dedicated to Me; they abide in Me, generating through the pride "I am He" a mental state (vṛtti) that always takes My form within their internal organs—which, having cast off all impurities of rajas and tamas, are exceedingly clear due to the predominance of sattva. I am He.
I exist as a reflection within their mental states, which are exceedingly clear;
the word "ca" (and) has the sense of restriction, meaning "I am in them alone" and "they are in me alone.
For this is the very nature of a clear substance: that it assumes the form of whatever it is connected with.
Furthermore, it is the very nature of an object connected with a transparent substance that it reflects therein;
likewise, it is the very nature of even a non-transparent substance that it does not assume the form of what is connected to it;
and it is the very nature of an object connected with a non-transparent substance that it does not reflect therein.
For just as the light of the sun, though present everywhere, is manifested only in a clear surface such as a mirror and not in an unclear object such as a jar,
yet because of that it neither feels attachment toward the mirror nor aversion toward the jar;

even so, although I am equal toward all, being manifested in the clear mind of a devotee and unmanifested in the unclear mind of one lacking devotion, I do not feel attachment toward anything whatsoever.
Nor do I hate anyone;
for that which arises through the constraints of causal totality (sāmagrī) cannot be subject to blame.
This lack of partiality is to be explained in the same way as fire or the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru). //29//

Viśvanātha: [Objection] "But surely you grant liberation only to devotees and not to non-devotees; if so, do you not also possess partiality caused by attachment, aversion, and the like? [Reply] He says, "I am equal," to show that this is not so.

In the explanation that "those devotees abide in me, and I also abide in them," there is no distinction whatsoever: the Blessed One indeed abides in the entire world, and the Blessed One indeed abides in all beings.
Therefore, according to the principle stated in *Gītā* 4.11, "In whatever way people surrender unto me, in that same way do I favor them."
Just as they remain attached to me as devotees, so too am I attached to them; this is how it should be explained.

In this regard, the analogy of the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) and the like should be understood only in a partial sense; for those who have taken refuge in the wish-fulfilling tree do not become attached out of a longing for its fruits.
Nor is the wish-fulfilling tree attached to those who depend upon it,
nor does it harbor hatred toward an enemy of its dependents;
yet the Blessed One, by his own hand, strikes down even the enemy of his own devotee.

Regarding what was said to Prahlāda— "When he would do harm, I shall destroy even him who is strengthened by boons"— some explain that the particle *tu* signifies a change in the initial subject matter; they maintain that the partiality characterized by affection for devotees indeed exists in Me, and that this is an ornament of the Blessed Lord, not a defect.
For it is well known that the Blessed One possesses affection specifically for His devotees, but not for those who possess mere knowledge or for yogis;
just as another person is affectionate only toward his own servants and not toward the servants of others.
In the same way, the Blessed One is also affectionate only toward his own devotees, and not toward the devotees of Rudra nor toward the devotees of the Goddess. //29//

Baladeva: But surely you lead only the devotees to your presence and not the non-devotees; does this not constitute a partiality on your part, even though you are the Lord of all, caused by attachment and aversion?
To this he replies: "I am equal."

Among all beings—whether gods, humans, animals, or stationary objects—who are diverse in terms of species, form, and nature, I, the Lord of All, am impartial in creating and sustaining them according to their respective past actions; just as the rain-cloud acts toward various kinds of seeds, there is no one among them who is either hateful or dear to Me. This is the meaning.
In this context, however, the word "tu" (but) is used to indicate the distinction of devotees from non-devotees:
those who worship me— that is, who favor me through devotional acts such as hearing and so forth— abide in me through their devotion and attachment.
Among them, even I, though the Lord of all, abide with devotion;
according to the analogy of the jewel and gold, the Blessed One also possesses devotion toward His devotees.
This specific excellence of mutual conduct out of love is demonstrated by the words of Śrī Śuka, such as "The Blessed One is possessed of devotion for His devotees," and so forth.
Otherwise, however, there would be the consequence of non-distinction;
for his proposition is understood to be exactly as follows, beginning with the words "those who [perceive] me in whatever way," and so forth.
The analogy of the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpa-druma*) is also only partial in this regard; for in that case, there is no mutual affection and no perception of partiality.
Thus it has been said: "Even though I am impartial toward all, there exists a partiality characterized by parental affection (*vātsalya*) toward those who have taken refuge in me."
Thus says the author of the Sūtra: "It arises and it is perceived" (Vs 2.1.37).

Now, one might object: since devotion (*bhakti*) is also an action (*karman*), and because of the affection for that [devotion] toward those [objects], the definition [of perception] does not apply to it. To this we say: it is not so.
Because devotion (*bhakti*), as a manifestation of the power of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*), is distinct from ritual action (*karman*).
Furthermore, scripture states: "Devotion (*bhakti-yoga*) abides in that which has the single flavor of existence, consciousness, and bliss" (GTU 2.78).
Nor should it be argued that this [distinction] is a flaw because [devotion] is prompted by the essential nature itself.
Because it is praised for its excellence of qualities. //29//
Even if one of very wicked conduct worships Me with undivided devotion, he should be regarded as righteous indeed, for he has rightly resolved. (9.30)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, showing that this is the inconceivable power of devotion to Me alone, He says "api cet" (even if).

Even if a man is extremely wicked in conduct, if he—without [worshiping] separate deities as distinct [from Me], but with the realization that Vāsudeva alone is the deity—does not worship other deities but worships Me, the Supreme Lord, then he should be considered a saintly person, indeed the most excellent.
For he, having rightly resolved, made a noble determination, thinking: "By the worship of the Supreme Lord alone, I shall become one who has achieved his purpose. //30//
Madhusūdana: Furthermore, this is the very greatness of devotion to Me—that it produces a distinction even among equals. Listen to that greatness as well [in the verse beginning with] "api cet":

if anyone, even one of very wicked conduct like Ajāmila, being devoted to no other, worships Me—serves Me due to some rise of good fortune—he is to be considered truly virtuous even if he was previously unrighteous;
for (hi) he is one whose resolve is firm (samyag-vyavasitaḥ), possessing the certainty of the virtuous. //30//
Viśvanātha:
My attachment toward my own devotees is entirely natural;
it does not depart even from a devotee who is ill-behaved.
Thinking, "I shall make even him most excellent," he says, "api cet" (even if).
Even if one is of very bad conduct—intent on harming others, seizing the wives and wealth of others, and so forth—if he worships me, what kind of worship does he possess? To this he says:
One who does not resort to anything other than Me— neither another deity distinct from Me,
nor any action, knowledge, or the like other than devotion to Me,
nor any desire for kingship and so forth other than the desire for Me— is a saintly person.
Now, when such conduct is observed, how can there be goodness?
To this he says: it must be considered—that is, it is to be reflected upon.
The meaning is that he is to be known precisely as a virtuous person; "he must be so regarded" is an injunctive statement, for otherwise there would be a transgression.
The underlying sense is that my command alone is the authoritative standard in this matter.
One might object: "Should he not be considered virtuous in the respect that he serves you, yet non-virtuous in the respect that he takes another's wife and so forth? To this, he says "evam" (thus).
He must be considered virtuous in every respect;
the sense is that his lack of virtue should never be perceived.
He whose resolve is "rightly determined" is one who has made a firm decision;

the meaning is that he has formed a beautiful resolution, thinking: "Though I may go to hell or the womb of animals due to my own sin which is so difficult to abandon, I shall by no means give up the exclusive worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Baladeva says: "My very nature, characterized by being subject to pure devotion, is indeed difficult to abandon."
Fulfilling the meaning of the previous verse by stating, "Even if I am attached to one who performs loathsome deeds, I shall exalt him," he says, "Even if" (api cet).

If a person who has no other devotion—even if he is of very bad conduct and his actions are extremely censurable—worships me, serving me through the chanting of my glories and so forth, then he too must be considered truly virtuous.

The meaning is that, because he does not worship or take refuge in any deity other than me, he is my single-minded devotee (*mad-ekāntī*), knowing me alone as his master and the supreme goal of human life.
The particle *eva* is used precisely to indicate that even if one acts in either of these two ways, such a person is to be honored as being virtuous (*sādhutvena*).
Furthermore, by the phrase "he should reflect upon his being thus," an injunction in the form of a personal command (*sva-nideśa-rūpa*) is shown;
the underlying intention is that otherwise, there would be a transgression (*pratyavāya*).
In both cases, the correctness of the present tense is indeed established; thus, nourishing the reason stated here, he says "samyak" (properly).
The meaning is that he is one who has made a correct resolve—that is, one possessing the most excellent certainty characterized by exclusive devotion to Me alone.
This has been stated in the Nārasiṃha Purāṇa:
A man whose mind is focused on no other than the Blessed Lord Hara shines brilliantly even if he is dark-skinned;
for one with a complexion as pale as a hare never does.
The moon undergoes defeat by the darkness. //30//
He quickly becomes righteous in soul and attains eternal peace.
O son of Kuntī, declare this with certainty: my devotee never perishes. (9.31)
