Śrīdhara: [Objection: But how can one be considered virtuous merely by having correct resolve? To this he says "quickly" (*kṣipram*). Even one of very bad conduct, by worshipping me, quickly becomes one whose mind is fixed on righteousness (*dharma*).
And from that, he goes to—that is, attains—eternal peace, which consists in the cessation of the mind's agitation and culminates in the Supreme Lord.

Fearing that those who argue with the harshness of fallacious reasoning might not accept this, [the Lord] encourages Arjuna, who was thus filled with doubt, saying: "O son of Kuntī, having gone to the assembly of those disputing preceded by the great sound of drums and the like, raise your arm and speak without hesitation."
Make a solemn declaration; pledge yourself thus:
"Even one who is a devotee of Me, the Supreme Lord, though he may be of very wicked conduct, does not perish;
rather, he surely attains his goal."
And then, their fallacious arguments having been utterly destroyed by the full manifestation of your maturity, they would undoubtedly take refuge in you alone as their teacher. //31//

Madhusūdana: "Precisely because of this right resolve, having abandoned wicked conduct, he quickly"—meaning that even one whose soul has long been unrighteous, by the power of devotion to Me, becomes very swiftly, in an instant, a righteous-souled one; that is to say, with a mind following dharma, having instantly cast off wickedness, he becomes one of virtuous conduct.

Furthermore, through extreme world-weariness, a certain devotee of Yours attains—indeed, reaches completely—eternal peace, which is the cessation of desire for the enjoyment of sense objects. One might think that such a person, not having abandoned previously practiced misconduct, could not be a righteous soul (*dharmātmā*) and would thus surely perish; to this, the Lord, as if provoked by being overcome with compassion for His devotees, says "no."
O Kaunteya, you should not consider this a wonder; such is the greatness of devotion to Me, as is certain.
Therefore, even in the presence of those who hold contrary views, you should declare it—make your proclamation with disdain and pride:

"Even one who is of extremely wicked conduct, even one fallen into a crisis of life, even one who is unworthy, even one who is crying out in distress, even one who is utterly deluded and without refuge—if he has devotion to Me, Vāsudeva, he does not perish."
Rather, one indeed becomes one who has accomplished their purpose.
The examples of Ajāmila, Prahlāda, Dhruva, Gajendra, and others are well known.
And the scripture states: "No inauspiciousness exists anywhere for those who are devotees of Vāsudeva. (31)

Viśvanātha: [Objection: "But how can you accept the worship of such a person who is not a qualified recipient (*adharmī*)? How can you eat the food, drink, and so forth offered by one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is defiled by lust, anger, and the like? To this he says: "He quickly—that is, very swiftly—becomes a righteous soul (*dharmātmā*).

Here, instead of using the forms *bhāvī* (future) or *gamiṣyati* (will go), which would mean "he will become a righteous soul" or "he will attain eternal peace," the words *bhavati* (becomes) and *gacchati* (goes) are employed to indicate that these states occur immediately.
Because of his present application, immediately after committing an unrighteous act, he remembers me and, filled with remorse, quickly becomes righteous in nature.
"Alas, alas! There is no one more base than this person who defiles the world of my devotees;
may I know him [to be so]. Thinking thus, he repeatedly and constantly attains peace and profound detachment.
Or rather, even at that time when his nature as Dharma is about to manifest after some period has passed, it indeed exists in a subtle form;
thus, through the entry of devotion into the mind, it is like the burning heat of a fever that, though in a state of subsiding for some duration, persists while a great medicine has been drunk.
The implied meaning (*dhvani*) is that even if the burning of poison is occurring, it is not taken into account.

Consequently, the secondary implication (*anudhvani*) is that for that devotee, lust, anger, and the like—which indicate a state of misconduct—are to be understood as utterly powerless, like a snake whose fangs have been pulled out.
Therefore, he constantly and at all times attains peace—that is, the complete subsiding of lust, anger, and so forth—and thus, even in a state of misconduct, his inner heart remains entirely pure.
This is the intended meaning.
Now, if he were a person of virtuous character (*dharmātmā*), then there would be no dispute at all;
however, there is someone who is a devotee of misconduct (*durācāra*) who does not abandon his wickedness even unto death.
"What is his condition?"—anticipating this question, the Lord, who is affectionate toward His devotees, spoke with maturity and as if with feigned anger, addressing him as "Kaunteya":
"My devotee does not perish;
even in the loss of life, he does not fall into the lower realms."
Fearing that those who argue with the harshness of fallacious reasoning might not accept this, the Lord encourages Arjuna, who is agitated by grief and apprehension:
"O Kaunteya, go to the assembly of those disputing amidst the great clamor of drums, trumpets, and other instruments; raising your arm, declare it without hesitation—make your solemn vow."
How so? Even one who is ill-behaved, if he is a devotee of Me, the Supreme Lord, shall not perish; rather, he becomes one who has achieved his purpose.

Consequently, having their fallacious arguments shattered by the manifestation of such maturity, they will undoubtedly take refuge in You alone as their guru—so says the venerable teacher (Svāmī-Caraṇa).
Now, one might ask: why did the Blessed Lord Himself, without making a formal promise, merely instruct Arjuna to make the promise?

"Just as [the Lord] will say, 'I declare the truth to you: you shall come to Me alone; you are dear to Me,' so too here, O Kaunteya, why was it not said: 'I declare to you that My devotee does not perish'?
It is replied: At that time, the Blessed One, who is affectionate toward His devotees, reflected: "By Me, who am devoted to My own devotees, even the slightest trace of deficiency in My devotee..."
In many instances, even by disregarding His own vow and accepting the exhaustion of His own sleep, He protected the vow of His devotee;
for example, in that very same Bhīṣma battle, setting aside His own vow, He will protect the vow of Bhīṣma.
For those outward-looking disputants and cavillers, upon hearing My vow, will laugh, thinking, "Arjuna’s vow is like a line etched in stone," and they perceive it thus.
"Therefore, I shall cause Arjuna himself to fulfill his vow.

Regarding this, because even one of such wicked conduct is heard to possess exclusive devotion (*ananya-bhakti*), the interpretation offered by the foolish scholars—that in all statements defining "exclusive devotion" there must be an absence of attachment to other women, children, and so forth, as well as an absence of unrighteousness, grief, delusion, lust, anger, and the like—is not to be accepted. //31//
Baladeva says:
"Thus, even one of very wicked conduct, by worshipping Me, quickly becomes righteous in mind;
and from that, he attains—reaches—eternal peace, which consists in the cessation of mental disturbances and is characterized by steadfast devotion to the Supreme Lord."
Fearing that those who argue with the harshness of fallacious reasoning might not acknowledge this [truth] within themselves, the Lord encourages Arjuna, who is filled with doubt: "O Kaunteya,
having gone to the assembly of those disputing preceded by the great sound of drums and other instruments, raise your arm and, free from hesitation,
make a solemn declaration."
How so? Even one who is a devotee of Me, the Supreme Lord, though he may be of very wicked conduct, does not perish;
rather, he becomes one who has achieved his purpose.
Consequently, having had their fallacious arguments shattered by the manifestation of Your maturity, they will undoubtedly take refuge in You alone as their Guru. //31//
For even those of sinful birth— women, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras— who take refuge in Me, O Pārtha, they too attain the supreme goal. (9.32)
Śrīdhara: What is surprising here that my devotion purifies one who has fallen from proper conduct?

For my devotion liberates even those of base birth and those who are ineligible from the cycle of worldly existence; thus he says, "For even those..."—even those who may be of sinful origin, meaning those of low birth such as the *antyajas* and others.

Even those Vaiśyas who are solely devoted to agriculture and the like, as well as women and Śūdras who are devoid of Vedic study and other such duties— even they, by taking refuge in me and serving me, attain the supreme goal.
For "hi" means "certainly. //32//

Madhusūdana: Having thus described the deliverance of those corrupted by adventitious defects through the power of devotion to the Lord, He now speaks of that same deliverance even for those corrupted by innate defects, beginning with "māṃ hi. "Hi" means certainly. O Pārtha, having sought refuge in Me by taking Me as their shelter—even those who may be of sinful birth, such as outcasts or animals, who are corrupted by the defect of their birth;
likewise, women, Vaiśyas, and others who are lowly due to being devoid of Vedic study and similar duties, and who are devoted solely to agriculture and the like.
Likewise, even Śūdras—who by birth and due to the absence of study and so forth are unfit for the supreme goal—attain that supreme goal;
by the use of the word "even" (api), it is implied that those of previously mentioned wicked conduct also attain it. //32//
Viśvanātha: What wonder is there that my devotion does not take account of the adventitious defects of those of evil conduct through their actions?

For this reason, he says "me," indicating that my devotion does not take account even of the natural defects of those who are evil by birth—those of sinful origin, such as the lowest castes and barbarians. As it has been said:
The Kirātas, Hūṇas, Āndhras, Pulindas, Pulkasas, Ābhīras, Śumbhas, Yavanas, Khasas, and others—
whatever other wicked people there may be who take refuge in him as their support.
"They are purified; salutation to that Sovereign Lord.
"Oh, how wonderful! Even a dog-eater is more venerable than one upon whose tongue-tip Your name does not reside."
The noble ones performed austerities, offered oblations, bathed, recited the Veda, and chanted Your names;
how much more so, then, those such as women and Vaiśyas who possess impurity, falsehood, and the like? (32)
Baladeva said: "Go to the assembly of those disputing with a great clamor, raise your arm, and make this vow without hesitation: 'I am the Lord of All;
I shake off the adventitious defects of those who are exclusively devoted to Me. What is so wonderful in this?
That even the most sinful are liberated, their ignorance shaken off through association with My devotees," he says with the words beginning "mām hi."

Even those of sinful birth, the outcastes, who are by nature of evil conduct—even they, through association with My devotees, take refuge in Me, the Lord of All, the son of Vasudeva; having sought shelter, they certainly attain the supreme goal, which is My own attainment, and which is difficult even for yogis to reach.
This is indeed certain.
Thus spoke the illustrious Śuka:
"The Kirātas, Hūṇas, Āndhras, Pulindas, Pulkasas, Ābhīras, Śumbhas, Yavanas, Khasas, and others— "
"Salutation to that Sovereign Lord, by taking refuge in whom even other sinners are purified.
By thus explicitly stating the impermanence of this world, Hari refutes its reality. //32//
How much more so, then, the meritorious Brahmins and likewise the devoted royal sages!
Having reached this transient and joyless world, do you worship me. (9.33)

Śrīdhara: Since this is so, what need is there to say that those of noble lineage and virtuous conduct who are my devotees attain the supreme goal? Thus he says, "What then... The term *puṇyāḥ* refers to the meritorious Brāhmaṇas;
likewise, *rājānaḥ* refers to kings, and *ṛṣayaḥ* refers to Kṣatriyas.
The meaning is: what more need be said about those who, being such as these, go to the supreme goal?
Therefore, having attained and obtained this body in the form of a royal sage, worship Me.

Furthermore, having reached this mortal world—which is impermanent, unstable, and devoid of happiness—do not delay because of its impermanence, and abandon all effort for the sake of pleasure because of its lack of happiness; [instead, worship] Me.
The meaning is: "Worship him in this very way. //33//

Madhusūdana: If this is so—that meritorious persons of virtuous conduct and noble birth, namely the Brāhmaṇas, as well as the royal sages (rājarṣis) who are discerners of subtle matters, being Kṣatriyas, attain the supreme goal when they are my devotees—then what more need be said?
The meaning is that there is no room for doubt on this point for anyone.

Since such is the greatness of devotion to Me, having obtained with great effort this human body— which is capable of accomplishing all human goals, yet extremely rare, impermanent, swiftly perishable, devoid of true happiness, and filled with manifold sufferings such as dwelling in the womb— worship Me as your refuge and take shelter of Me very quickly, before this body perishes.

Because this [human birth] is impermanent and fragile, do not delay, nor exert yourself for the sake of worldly pleasure; you are a royal sage, therefore make yourself fruitful by devoting yourself to Me.
Otherwise, such a birth as yours would indeed be fruitless—this is the meaning. //33//
Viśvanātha: Furthermore, how much more so then for those Brahmins who are meritorious, of noble lineage, and of virtuous conduct, and who are my devotees? Therefore, you should worship me. //33//
Baladeva said: "What do you mean?
If this is so, then what more need be said regarding those Brahmins, royal sages, and Kshatriyas of noble lineage who are meritorious, of virtuous conduct, and devoted; they attain the supreme goal.
There is not even a trace of doubt in this matter."

Therefore, you too, O royal sage, having reached this world, worship me; abandon your longing for sovereignty in this world which is impermanent, perishable, unhappy, possessing only slight happiness, and subject to destruction; instead, by worshipping me, attain me who am eternal and infinite bliss—this is the intent expressed here with urgency.
In this [verse], Hari explicitly declares the impermanence of this world, thereby refuting its falsity. //33//
Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me.
Thus, with your self disciplined and making Me your supreme goal, you shall come to Me alone. 34.
Śrīdhara: Demonstrating the manner of devotion, he concludes with the words "man-manāḥ. One whose mind is fixed on Me alone is "man-manāḥ"; become such as that.
Likewise, become My devotee—that is, My servant.
Sacrifice to Me; be habituated to My worship;
and bow down to Me alone.

Thus, by these means, being devoted to Me as the supreme goal, having yoked the self—the mind—to Me and concentrated it, you shall come to Me, that is, you shall attain Me who am the form of supreme bliss. //34//
In the ninth chapter, titled "The Secret of the King," Acyuta out of compassion spoke of His own wondrous sovereignty and the marvelous majesty of devotion.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Royal Science and the Royal Secret," in the *Subodhinī*, a commentary on the *Bhagavad-gītā* composed by the venerable Śrīdhara Svāmī.

Madhusūdana concludes by showing the manner of devotion with the words, "Be one whose mind is fixed on Me" (*man-manā bhava*). For even a king’s servant who is devoted to the king may have his mind directed toward his son and others; thus, though he is "fixed on him," he is not truly his devotee. Therefore, it is said: "Be one whose mind is fixed on Me, My devotee. Likewise, "be My worshiper" (*mad-yājī*), meaning one whose nature is the worship of Me; "bow down to Me" with mind, speech, and body.

Thus, by these means, being devoted to Me and having Me as your sole refuge, you shall— having disciplined the self, that is, the internal organ, and concentrated it upon Me— attain and reach Me alone, who am a mass of supreme bliss, self-luminous, devoid of all affliction, and fearless. //34//
Those whose hearts are purified by tasting the nectar of the lotus feet of Śrī Govinda cross the ocean of saṃsāra at once; they behold the full effulgence,
they ascertain the supreme good through the Vedāntas, and they abandon delusion.
Those who are pure perceive duality as being like a dream and attain a state of stainless bliss.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Sovereign Knowledge and the Sovereign Secret," according to the distinction of qualified aspirants, in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā-Gūḍhārtha-Dīpikā* (The Lamp Illuminating the Hidden Meaning of the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā) composed by Śrī Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, disciple of the feet of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Viśveśvara Sarasvatī. //9//
Viśvanātha: Showing the manner of devotion, he concludes with the words "man-manā" (with mind on Me).
Thus, having yoked—that is, having directed—the self, the mind, and the body toward Me. //34//
The capacity to discern between worthy and unworthy recipients, and the purification of all through one's own touch—
this is seen here as the royal secret of devotion alone.
Thus, in the *Harṣiṇī* commentary that showers the essence of meaning for those whose hearts are devoted, the ninth chapter has been properly concluded for the virtuous. 9.
Baladeva: Now, instructing Arjuna—who has reached the final stage—in his desired pure devotion, the Lord concludes with the words "man-manā" (with mind fixed on Me).

Even one who is devoted to a king may have his mind fixed on his wife and so forth; likewise, even if one's mind is fixed on that [object], he does not become truly devoted to it. You, however, by means of a disposition distinct from those, be "man-manā," that is, be My devotee.

He whose mind is constantly like an uninterrupted stream of honey, characterized by the thought of me—Vasudeva’s son, endowed with qualities such as the dark hue of a blue lotus—as his own master and the goal of his human life;
likewise, become a worshiper of me, devoted to the adoration of me who am so exceedingly dear to him;
and bow down to such a me with great love, prostrating yourself like a staff.
Thus, having disciplined yourself and offered your self, mind, and body unto Me, being devoted to Me and having Me as your sole refuge, you shall come to Me;
it should be understood that this very devotion must be performed as an offering. //34//
"Devoid of the discrimination between worthy and unworthy recipients, devotion that destroys all sins through mere contact is remembered here as the secret of kings, being like the Gaṅgā itself."
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā Upaniṣad. //9//

[*ENDNOTE] With the highest praise, I, together with the hosts of Maruts, perpetually propitiate that one Govinda, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, who is composed of five parts, and who sits beneath the trees of Vṛndāvana.
